social.name: income & work
social.levelRationale: Anchor: 61.8% of New Yorkers (5.04M of 8.16M) fall below the City's own True Cost of Living threshold, against an implied target of 0% — the threshold is by definition the income needed to be independent of public and private assistance, and Charter Amendment 3 (Nov 2022, 81% approval) mandates the City to measure and report it annually. 13% of residents (~1M people) are below even HALF the threshold, and government transfers close only ~5 percentage points of the gap (67% pre-transfer to 62% post). An independent measure on a different methodology agrees on the order of magnitude: FCNY's Self-Sufficiency Standard puts 46% of working-age households below its threshold on 2024 incomes. R1 upward adjustments: Poverty Tracker at a record 26% in 2024 (2.2M people, twice the national rate); 2024 Gini of 0.5563, now second-highest among large US cities (up from 4th); Bronx good-job rate of 20% vs 46% in Manhattan; Black unemployment 8.9% (Dec 2025), over 3x white, with young Black workers at 23.8% (2024); and a 66-point neighborhood spread on the TCOL measure itself (80% in Mott Haven/Hunts Point to 14% in the Financial District). R1 downward adjustments, weighed and named: the FCNY series shows inadequacy falling from its 2021 peak (though still above pre-pandemic, and RISING for single-full-time-earner households, 40%→44%); citywide unemployment a moderate 5.2% (2025 annual average); real median household income up 2.2% in 2024; and the strongest actively-enforced municipal labour-standards regime in the country ($17 minimum wage, $22.13 delivery-worker floor upheld twice in federal court in Jan 2026, Fair Workweek with $8.5M recovered since Jan 2026, statewide Freelance Isn't Free). Those are why this is 100 rather than 130 or 150 — they are policy responses and a moderating trend, not evidence that a majority of the city can currently cover basic needs — and they do not support anything below 100. Caveat capping confidence rather than level: the headline is 2022-vintage data published in 2026.
social.indicator: NYC True Cost of Living (TCOL) Measure — share of residents below the true cost of living threshold
social.value: 55.6% below the TCOL threshold — below the citywide 61.8% — but the widest racial gap of any borough: Hispanic 85.3%, Black 79.7%, Asian/PI 54.5%, White 32.9%, a 52-point Hispanic-white spread against 35 points in the Bronx. Also the highest average resource gap of any borough ($44,529) and the second-highest deep-hardship rate in the city (15.2% below half the threshold), reflecting economic polarization; 57.8% of persons in families with children.
social.target: The TCOL threshold is itself the benchmark: implied target 0% of residents below it. Charter Amendment 3 (November 2022, approved by 81% of voters — the third of three racial justice ballot measures) mandates the City to create and annually report a measure of what it actually costs to live in New York City, and the measure defines the threshold as 'the resources necessary for individuals and families to be independent of public and private assistance.' The report itself states no numeric reduction target. Independent cross-check: FCNY/United Way/Center for Women's Welfare Self-Sufficiency Standard, 46% of working-age households below its threshold (2024 incomes, 2026 costs). Secondary equity benchmark: MOERJ's Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan goal of closing racial TCOL gaps (Hispanic 77.6%, Black 65.6%, Asian/Pacific Islander 63.3%, White 43.7%).
social.context:
Manhattan: 55.6% below the TCOL threshold — below the citywide 61.8% — but the widest racial gap of any borough: Hispanic 85.3%, Black 79.7%, Asian/PI 54.5%, White 32.9%, a 52-point Hispanic-white spread against 35 points in the Bronx. Also the highest average resource gap of any borough ($44,529) and the second-highest deep-hardship rate in the city (15.2% below half the threshold), reflecting economic polarization; 57.8% of persons in families with children.

Citywide for comparison: 61.8% of New Yorkers (5.04M of 8.16M residents) below the TCOL threshold citywide, measured AFTER government supports; 67% before supports, i.e. transfers close ~5 percentage points. Universe is persons in families, all ages. A further 3.58M New Yorkers are above the federal poverty line but still below the TCOL threshold (the 'missing middle'), and 13% of residents (~1M people) are below HALF the threshold. Families with children face a median cost of $159,197/yr against median resources of $124,007 (78% of cost), an average gap of $35,190 — of which market resources supply $95,277 and government transfers $28,730. Citywide, persons in families below the threshold have an average annual resource gap of $39,603 (median costs $122,919 vs median resources $78,993). 73% of NYC children (1.2M) live in families below the threshold, rising to 86.8% in the Bronx. The highest rate of any group: 92% of people in families with a self-care disability (working-age adults under 65), with an average gap of $76,178; the broader any-disability rates are 80.3% (under 65) and 68.1% (65+).

A purpose-built official city measure rather than a federal proxy, mandated by Charter Amendment 3 (Nov 2022) and published in its inaugural edition by MOERJ with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute — report dated March 2026, released April 6, 2026 as part of the Mamdani administration's first-100-days package. VINTAGE CAVEAT (important): all estimates come from the Urban Institute's ATTIS model applied to 2018 American Community Survey data projected to 2022, so this is a 2022-vintage estimate published in 2026, with a population base of 8.16M residents. The measure adapts the Urban Institute's True Cost of Economic Security framework and, unlike the NYCgov poverty measure, asks what it takes to be independent of assistance rather than whether a poverty threshold is met — the report is explicit that the two are complementary rather than directly comparable. The threshold includes housing, food, health care, child care, transportation, taxes, a savings target set at 10% of expenses, and other necessities. RECONCILIATION with the other 'True Cost of Living' series (per R11): FCNY/United Way's NYC True Cost of Living reports 46% of WORKING-AGE HOUSEHOLDS below threshold (2024 ACS 1-year PUMS, incomes adjusted to 2026 costs), and 50% in its 2023 report (1,298,212 households, 2,991,973 people) against 36% in 2021. The 16-point gap to 62% is not a discrepancy but four definitional differences: unit (persons vs households), universe (all residents vs working-age households, FCNY explicitly excluding adults 65+, group quarters, and adults with work-limiting disabilities — precisely MOERJ's highest-rate groups), threshold basket (savings target included vs Self-Sufficiency Standard with none), and vintage (2022 vs 2024/2026). Note the direction check: FCNY measures resources BEFORE any assistance and still lands lower than MOERJ's post-transfer figure, confirming transfers are not the driver of the gap. TREND: the FCNY series is the only one with a real time trend and it declined 2012-2019, rose sharply in 2021, and declined again by 2024 — still 'substantially higher than pre-pandemic levels, despite declining from the 2021 peak.' FCNY attributes the decline to composition rather than easing affordability: fewer no-worker households as the labour market recovered, and a 1.2pp fall in the share of households with children (who face higher thresholds). Critically, inadequacy among households with one full-time year-round worker ROSE from 40% (2021) to 44% (2024), and rose among all working households — full-time work is increasingly insufficient. The scale dwarfs a small city like Petaluma: a majority of an 8.2M-person city cannot cover basic needs while working, and the Hispanic-white gap (77.6% vs 43.7%) is itself wider than the entire gap between Petaluma's poverty rate and the US average. Policy levers: MOERJ's Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan (45 agencies, 200+ goals, 800+ strategies) and the Council's '30 For Our City' minimum-wage bill.
social.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)
actions: Testify or submit written comment to the NYC Council on the '30 For Our City' minimum-wage bill (Council Member Sandy Nurse's office), which would take the city floor to $20/hr by 2027 and $30/hr by 2030 for large employers.

Report Fair Workweek scheduling violations, delivery-worker underpayment below the $22.13/hr floor, or freelance nonpayment to NYC's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) worker-rights portal — DCWP has recovered over $8.5M in restitution since January 2026 and $5.195M for delivery workers alone.

Apply for 3-K and Pre-K for All seats through NYC Public Schools, or for a child care voucher through the Administration for Children's Services, to offset the child care barrier the TCOL Measure identifies as a top-three cost driver for families with children.

Engage with the Mayor's Office of Equity & Racial Justice's public process on the Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan, which sets the framework for closing the TCOL racial gaps (Hispanic 77.6% vs White 43.7%).

Support NY Senate Bill S173 (Unemployment Bridge Program) to give excluded and undocumented workers a permanent safety net, replacing the 2021 Excluded Workers Fund that lapsed after paying out more than $2B to 130,000+ workers.

Track the NYC Comptroller's pension-fund shareholder campaign pressing banks — including NYC-headquartered JPMorgan Chase, the world's largest fossil-fuel financier at $58B in 2025, and Citigroup — on financed-emissions disclosure and net-zero asset-manager compliance.

social.neighborhoodNote: The sharpest disaggregation available is on the dimension's own indicator rather than a proxy: FCNY's 'Overlooked & Undercounted in New York City 2026' reports the share of households below the True Cost of Living ranging from 80% in Bronx Community Districts 1 & 2 (Melrose, Mott Haven, Longwood, Hunts Point) to 14% in Manhattan Community Districts 1 & 2 (Financial District, Greenwich Village) — a 66-point spread, and arguably the single sharpest income-and-work disparity in the portrait. The same brief finds 86% of single mothers with young children below the threshold, and notes that 40% of households have at least one child in Bronx CDs 1 & 2 versus 19% in Manhattan CDs 1 & 2. Federal-poverty contrast, from the 2024 ACS: citywide 18.0%, Bronx 28.8%, Brooklyn 19.2%, Manhattan 15.6%, Queens 13.3%, Staten Island 11.1% — the Bronx remains the poorest large urban county in the nation on conventional measures.

subIndicators.name: FCNY/United Way NYC True Cost of Living (independent co-measure, Self-Sufficiency Standard)
subIndicators.value: 46% of working-age NYC households below the True Cost of Living (15% below the Official Poverty Measure plus a further 31% above poverty but still short of basic needs); 50% in the 2023 report (1,298,212 households, 2,991,973 people) and 36% in the 2021 report. Universe excludes adults 65+, group quarters and adults with work-limiting disabilities; measured with NO public or private assistance counted. Trend: declined 2012-2019, rose sharply in 2021, declined again by 2024, but remains substantially above pre-pandemic — and inadequacy among households with one full-time year-round worker ROSE from 40% (2021) to 44% (2024).
subIndicators.source: Center for Women's Welfare, University of Washington School of Social Work, for the Fund for the City of New York / United Way of NYC — 'Overlooked & Undercounted in New York City 2026' (March 18, 2026); 2024 ACS 1-year PUMS with incomes adjusted to 2026 cost benchmarks
subIndicators.note: Not interchangeable with the 61.8% MOERJ headline — different unit, universe, basket and vintage. See local.context for the full reconciliation.

subIndicators.name: Poverty Tracker (independent, Columbia University / Robin Hood Foundation)
subIndicators.value: 26% overall poverty rate in 2024 — twice the national rate and the highest since the Poverty Tracker began — affecting 2.2M people (1.7M adults, nearly 450,000 children); nearly 5 million New Yorkers, 3 in 5, live below 200% of the poverty line
subIndicators.source: Robin Hood / Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy, 'The State of Poverty and Disadvantage in New York City' Vol. 8 (released March 2026)
subIndicators.note: Vol. 7 (Feb 2025) reported 25% on 2023 data, 2.02M people — cite the correct volume when quoting.

subIndicators.name: Federal/ACS poverty rate (contrast measure)
subIndicators.value: 18.0% of persons at or below the federal poverty line citywide (2024 ACS), down 0.2pp from 2023 and 5.9 points above the US rate of 12.1%; by borough Bronx 28.8%, Brooklyn 19.2%, Manhattan 15.6%, Queens 13.3%, Staten Island 11.1%; by age under-18 24.2%, 18-64 15.4%, 65+ 20.2%. Race/ethnicity breakdown available only for 2023: Hispanic 24.8%, Black 21.7%, Asian 16.8%, White 11.5%.
subIndicators.source: U.S. Census Bureau 2024 ACS as compiled in NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026); 2023 race breakdown from Community Service Society of NY analysis of ACS

subIndicators.name: Gini index of income inequality (ACS B19083)
subIndicators.value: 0.5563 citywide (2024), up from 0.5546 in 2023 — the second-highest among large U.S. cities, behind only Miami (0.5637), against a U.S. coefficient of 0.4809; by borough Manhattan 0.5944, Brooklyn 0.5347, Bronx 0.5336, Queens 0.4694, Staten Island 0.4374
subIndicators.source: NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026), ACS B19083 vintage 2024

subIndicators.name: Median household income
subIndicators.value: $81,228 citywide (2024 ACS), up 6.1% nominally and 2.2% in real terms vs 2023; renter households $64,866 (+1.8% real), owner households $121,443 (-0.4% real). Renter income by borough rose most in Staten Island (+36.2% real) and Manhattan (+6.9%), and fell in the Bronx.
subIndicators.source: U.S. Census Bureau 2024 ACS as compiled in NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study'
subIndicators.note: Supersedes an earlier Furman-attributed citywide figure of $83,970 that could not be reconciled with the published 2024 ACS value; per R3 the published figure is used. A clean single-vintage five-borough median-household-income set was not assembled — the borough detail here is renter-income change, not level.

subIndicators.name: 'Good job' rate by borough (living wage + full-time year-round + employer health insurance + safe conditions)
subIndicators.value: Citywide 33.2%; Manhattan ~46%, Staten Island ~37%, Brooklyn ~33%, Queens ~28%, Bronx ~20%. A job counts only if it pays a living wage for the worker's household size, is 35+ hrs/week and 50+ weeks/year, carries employer-sponsored health insurance, and is either safe or pays a 25% hazard premium.
subIndicators.source: Office of the NYC Comptroller (Brad Lander), 'The State of Job Quality in New York City' (published May 14, 2025; 2017-2023 series). Mark Levine is the current Comptroller but did not issue this report.

subIndicators.name: Unemployment rate by race/ethnicity
subIndicators.value: Black 8.9%, Hispanic 6.3%, Asian 3.5%, White under 3% (December 2025) — the Black rate over 3x the white rate. Against December 2019: Hispanic was 4.9% (now 1.4 points higher) and Asian 1.8% (now 1.7 points higher); white unemployment is closest to pre-pandemic.
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, 'Post-Pandemic Unemployment in NYC Persists for Some Demographic Groups' (April 7, 2026 release, December 2025 data)

subIndicators.name: Youth unemployment
subIndicators.value: Young Black workers at 23.8% unemployment in 2024, nine points above 2019; overall 16-24 youth unemployment 13.2% in 2024, 3.6 points above 2019, with Black, Hispanic and Asian youth — especially young men — above the overall youth rate
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, 'Youth in NYC Face Double-Digit Unemployment Rate' (June 2025)

subIndicators.name: Unemployment rate by borough
subIndicators.value: Citywide annual average 5.2% in 2025, up 0.2pp from 5.0% in 2024 and 1.2 points above 2019; by borough Bronx 6.8% (consistently highest), Brooklyn 5.2%, Queens 4.6%, Manhattan 4.6%, Staten Island 4.5% (lowest). Rates fell 0.1-0.2pp in every borough. Latest month available: January 2026 at 5.5% citywide, 0.7pp above January 2025.
subIndicators.source: BLS / NYS Dept. of Labor Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), as published in NYC Rent Guidelines Board '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026)
subIndicators.note: Single-vintage official five-borough set; supersedes an earlier mixed-vintage third-party (FRED/Trading Economics) assembly whose Queens, Staten Island and Manhattan values were incorrect.

subIndicators.name: NY minimum wage in NYC
subIndicators.value: $17.00/hr effective Jan 1, 2026 (up from $16.50 in 2025) in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester; $16.00 in the rest of the state. Tipped food service workers $11.35 cash wage with a $5.65 tip credit; other tipped service employees $14.15 with a $2.85 credit. The statutory $0.50 step schedule ends with 2026; from 2027 the wage is indexed annually to CPI-W for the Northeast region.
subIndicators.source: NYS Department of Labor / Gov. Hochul minimum wage schedule (2023 state law)

subIndicators.name: App-based delivery worker minimum pay rate
subIndicators.value: $22.13/hr as of April 1, 2026, up from $21.44 — a 3.2% inflation adjustment for Dec 2024-Dec 2025 — covering both food and third-party grocery delivery workers; first-in-the-nation standard. Enforcement has produced a $5,195,000 settlement with Uber Eats, Fantuan and HungryPanda covering more than 49,000 workers (Uber Eats $3.15M restitution to 48,000+ plus $350K penalties for unpaid canceled-trip time Dec 2023-Sep 2024; HungryPanda $1,068,672 to 1,000+; Fantuan $468K+ to 285), plus Uber's agreement to reinstate as many as 10,000 wrongfully deactivated workers. DCWP is separately suing non-compliant platforms, having found Motoclick workers earning $3.67-$4.67/hr.
subIndicators.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)

subIndicators.name: Average Wall Street bonus vs. typical wage
subIndicators.value: $246,900 average bonus for 2025, up 6%, on a record $49.2B bonus pool; average total securities-industry compensation $505,677 in 2024, up 7.3% and the second-highest on record — roughly 5x the average private-sector salary elsewhere in the city. The securities sector accounted for 20.2% of all NYC economic activity in 2024, 8.4% of city tax revenue in City FY2025 and 19.4% of state tax collections in SFY2024-25, while 1 in 13 city jobs is directly or indirectly tied to it.
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, Wall Street bonus report (March 2026)

subIndicators.name: Freelance/gig workforce share
subIndicators.value: ~1.3 million people, ~34% of NYC's workforce, performed freelance work in the prior 12 months, generating an estimated $31.4B in annual earnings; 29% freelanced full-time, 50% part-time, 20% as supplemental income
subIndicators.source: Freelancers Union and Upwork with the NYC Mayor's Office of Media and Entertainment, 'Freelancing in New York City' (September 2019)
subIndicators.note: Pre-pandemic and seven years stale — the only comprehensive city-scale freelance estimate located. Treat as indicative only; no post-2019 update was found.

subIndicators.name: Childcare cost as labor-force barrier
subIndicators.value: Roughly 375,000 city parents left a job or reduced work commitments in 2022 due to inadequate child care access, at an estimated cost of $23 billion in lost economic output, $5.9 billion in lost disposable income and $2.2 billion in lost tax revenue. Quality care is unaffordable for 80% of NY families, at an average $26,000 per child annually and up to $40,000.
subIndicators.source: Citizens' Committee for Children of New York (CCC), 'NYC Needs Universal Child Care'

global.levelRationale: Two quantified transmission channels running outward from NYC, both worsening on the labour-and-capital side and only partially offset on the civic side. Capital allocation: JPMorgan Chase, headquartered in NYC, is the world's single largest fossil-fuel financier at $58B in 2025 (up 12.6%), with fellow NYC-headquartered Citigroup in the global top five at $45-47B; financing to companies actively EXPANDING fossil fuels surged 27% to $508B in 2025, the Net-Zero Banking Alliance collapsed, and JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs abandoned their coal and Arctic exclusions outright. Labour: roughly 412,000 undocumented New Yorkers remain excluded from unemployment insurance and much baseline labour-law protection, concentrated in the delivery, domestic-work, food-service and construction sectors that underpin the city's consumption, with no permanent successor to the lapsed 2021 Excluded Workers Fund. Offsetting, and real: NYC's own public pension funds run one of the most prominent divestment programmes in U.S. public finance, which survived final appellate review in October 2025 and beat its 2025 interim emissions target a year early (37% reduction 2019-2024). That contradiction between the city's private financial sector and its public capital is the finding, and it is critical-tier because the private side is the larger and growing quantity. Confidence is capped at medium because the remittance channel — the most on-dimension global-social flow for income & work — remains unquantified.
global.indicator: NYC's outward income-and-work footprint: workers excluded from labour protection inside the city, and NYC-headquartered banks' fossil-fuel capital allocation set against NYC public pension divestment
global.value: LABOUR CHANNEL: An estimated ~412,000 undocumented New Yorkers (NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs, 2022; down from ~611,000 in 2012; NYC Comptroller estimated ~476,000 in 2019) are excluded from unemployment insurance and many labour protections, and are disproportionately exposed to wage theft. New York State's 2021 Excluded Workers Fund distributed more than $2B of its $2.1B appropriation to more than 130,000 approved applicants — 99% receiving the Tier 1 benefit of $15,600 — before exhausting by December 2021, with no permanent successor enacted as of mid-2026. CAPITAL CHANNEL: JPMorgan Chase (HQ: NYC) financed $58B in fossil fuels in 2025, up 12.6% and the largest of any bank in the world; Citigroup (HQ: NYC) is in the global top five at roughly $45-47B. Of the 2025 top five, only JPMorgan and Citigroup are NYC-headquartered — Bank of America ($47B) is Charlotte, MUFG ($47B) and Mizuho are Tokyo. The world's 65 largest banks financed fossil fuels with $906B in 2025 (+8% year-over-year) and $8.7 trillion since the 2016 Paris Agreement, with financing to fossil-fuel expanders up 27% to $508B. CIVIC COUNTERWEIGHT: three of NYC's five public pension systems (Teachers' Retirement System, NYCERS, Board of Education Retirement System) voted to divest from publicly-traded fossil-fuel reserve owners in 2021 and completed divestment in 2022, added an upstream private-markets exclusion in 2023, and hold a 2040 net-zero portfolio target with a $50B climate-solutions goal by 2035; weighted-average financed Scope 1+2 emissions fell 37% between 2019 and 2024, beating the 2025 interim targets a year early. Litigation challenging the divestment (Wong et al. v. NYCERS) was dismissed for lack of standing, affirmed on appeal, and the New York Court of Appeals denied leave to appeal on October 21, 2025 — final. Divestment has NOT been reversed.
global.target: No binding target exists for NYC-headquartered banks' financed emissions — this is private-sector activity outside city jurisdiction. The closest civic-side commitments are the NYC pension funds' 2040 net-zero portfolio target and $50B-by-2035 climate-solutions goal (NYC Comptroller / Bureau of Asset Management). On the labour side, the aspirational benchmark is universal coverage: the proposed Unemployment Bridge Program (NY Senate Bill S173, 2025) as a permanent successor to the Excluded Workers Fund, which would extend unemployment-style support to excluded and undocumented workers.
global.context: NYC's global-social footprint in income & work runs through two channels. The labour channel is the on-dimension one: roughly 412,000 undocumented residents form part of an informal economy underpinning low-wage sectors that make the city's consumption possible, while remaining outside unemployment insurance and disproportionately exposed to wage theft — a transmission that also runs outward through the households and countries those workers support. The capital channel is the quantified one: the same city that hosts the world's largest fossil-fuel underwriter also manages, through its Comptroller-run pension funds, one of the most prominent divestment programmes in U.S. public finance, transmitted through securities underwriting and lending and through shareholder-engagement campaigns the Comptroller runs on banks the city does business with. Both are distinctly big-city phenomena with no Petaluma equivalent. CROSS-DIMENSION WARNING: the fossil-finance material is a climate transmission channel as much as an income-and-work one and is likely to appear in the climate change dimension's global lens; the orchestrator should decide where it lives to avoid double-counting. DATA GAPS: no credible NYC-specific dollar estimate for remittances sent abroad from the city could be located, which is the most obviously on-dimension global-social flow for this dimension and is flagged rather than estimated. Two live pension-policy statuses could not be confirmed and are stated as unresolved rather than asserted: whether trustees adopted the December 2024 proposal to exclude future private-market midstream/downstream fossil-fuel investment, and the outcome of the June 30, 2025 deadline for public-markets asset managers to file compliant net-zero plans.
global.source: Oil Change International / Rainforest Action Network et al., 'Banking on Climate Chaos 2026' (published June 8, 2026, covering 2025 data); NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs; NYC Comptroller's Office; NYS Department of Labor; NY State Senate

policyAnchors.name: NYC True Cost of Living Measure & Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan (2026)
policyAnchors.relevance: First official city-government TCOL measure and racial equity plan for income/work outcomes, mandated by Charter Amendment 3 of November 2022 (approved by 81% of voters, the third of three racial justice ballot measures); sets the baseline (61.8% below TCOL) used as this dimension's headline indicator, and the Charter requires annual reporting.
policyAnchors.status: Inaugural report dated March 2026, released April 6, 2026 by the Mamdani administration (Mayor's Office of Equity & Racial Justice under Chief Equity Officer and Commissioner Afua Atta-Mensah, appointed January 2026, with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute). The Racial Equity Plan is explicitly 'preliminary', with 45 agencies, 200+ goals and 800+ strategies still being finalized. Data vintage is 2022 (2018 ACS projected forward via the Urban Institute ATTIS model), so the next release should be watched for a genuine update.

policyAnchors.name: '30 For Our City' minimum wage bill (NYC Council)
policyAnchors.relevance: Would raise the NYC minimum wage well beyond the state-set floor — to $20/hr by 2027 and $30/hr by 2030 for employers with more than 500 employees, and $30/hr by 2032 for smaller employers. Would be the highest municipal minimum wage in the United States.
policyAnchors.status: Introduced by Council Member Sandy Nurse and announced March 10, 2026 under the 'Raise Up NY' banner, publicly backed by Mayor Mamdani and a bloc of Council members; under consideration in the Council with no full-Council vote as of late July 2026. Committee assignment not independently confirmed.

policyAnchors.name: NY State minimum wage schedule (2023 state law)
policyAnchors.relevance: Sets the current wage floor for NYC and the indexing mechanism beyond 2026.
policyAnchors.status: In effect: $17.00/hr in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester as of Jan 1, 2026; $16.00 in the rest of the state. State law schedules the last flat $0.50 step for 2026, then CPI-W (Northeast region) indexed annual increases beginning 2027.

policyAnchors.name: App-Based Delivery Workers' Minimum Pay Rate (NYC Local Law / DCWP rule, 2021-23, amended 2025-26)
policyAnchors.relevance: First-in-the-nation minimum pay standard for app-based food and grocery delivery workers.
policyAnchors.status: In effect and actively enforced; rate rose to $22.13/hr on April 1, 2026. Amended rules took effect January 26, 2026, extending minimum pay to grocery delivery workers, requiring up-front tipping options, written pay statements within seven days, and trip-distance disclosure. Industry challenges failed on both fronts in SDNY on or about January 22, 2026: Judge John Koeltl denied a preliminary injunction against the grocery-delivery minimum pay requirements and subsequently denied an injunction pending appeal, while Judge George Daniels denied injunctive relief against the up-front tipping framework, which platforms challenged as compelled speech. A request to stay proceedings pending appeal was still being adjudicated. DCWP has extracted a $5,195,000 settlement from Uber Eats, Fantuan and HungryPanda covering 49,000+ workers plus reinstatement of up to 10,000 deactivated workers, and is suing non-compliant platforms.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Fair Workweek Law (Local Laws 66-69 of 2017)
policyAnchors.relevance: Predictive-scheduling and just-cause protections for fast-food and retail workers, a major lever against income volatility for low-wage NYC workers.
policyAnchors.status: Actively enforced by DCWP under the Mamdani administration; more than $8.5M in restitution recovered since Jan 1, 2026, including a settlement of over $1.5M affecting 760+ workers (March 2026) and an action against a premium retailer (Theory LLC, ~$277K).

policyAnchors.name: Earned Safe and Sick Time Act (ESSTA) expansion
policyAnchors.relevance: Expands paid/unpaid safe-and-sick leave categories relevant to low-wage and gig-adjacent workers' income stability.
policyAnchors.status: Expanded provisions took effect Feb 22, 2026, adding up to 32 hours of frontloaded unpaid safe/sick leave atop existing paid leave (40-56 hrs depending on employer size), and new usable categories including housing court proceedings, workplace-violence recovery and disaster response.

policyAnchors.name: Freelance Isn't Free Act
policyAnchors.relevance: Protects freelance workers — roughly a third of the NYC workforce on the last comprehensive count — from nonpayment.
policyAnchors.status: NYC's 2016 local law was extended statewide effective Aug 28, 2024 (NY General Business Law Article 44-A); in effect, enforced by NYS DOL and NYC DCWP.

policyAnchors.name: City of Yes for Economic Opportunity
policyAnchors.relevance: Citywide zoning reform intended to expand job-creating business types and reduce regulatory barriers to work.
policyAnchors.status: Adopted by City Council June 6, 2024 under the Adams administration; zoning changes are permanent and remain in effect under the Mamdani administration, with continuing implementation (industrial strategic plan, enforcement resourcing commitments).

policyAnchors.name: Excluded Workers Fund (2021) / proposed Unemployment Bridge Program
policyAnchors.relevance: Precedent for extending unemployment-style support to undocumented and other excluded workers; its lapse is the central unresolved gap in labour protection for NYC's excluded workforce.
policyAnchors.status: The 2021 New York State fund appropriated $2.1B and distributed more than $2B to more than 130,000 approved applicants — 99% at the Tier 1 benefit of $15,600 — before exhausting by December 2021, and was never replaced. A permanent successor, the Unemployment Bridge Program (NY Senate Bill S173, 2025, proposed to be funded by a digital-advertising tax on large tech firms), had not been enacted as of mid-2026.

policyAnchors.name: NYC public pension fossil-fuel divestment and 2040 net-zero commitment
policyAnchors.relevance: The city's own capital is the one part of the finance channel NYC government directly controls; it is the counterweight to NYC-headquartered private banks' fossil-fuel financing in the global lens.
policyAnchors.status: In force and judicially settled. TRS, NYCERS and BERS voted to divest from publicly-traded fossil-fuel reserve owners in 2021 and completed divestment in 2022; an upstream private-markets exclusion was added in 2023; the 2040 net-zero portfolio target and a $50B-by-2035 climate-solutions goal stand, with weighted-average financed Scope 1+2 emissions down 37% between 2019 and 2024, beating the 2025 interim targets a year early. Wong et al. v. NYCERS was dismissed for lack of standing, affirmed on appeal, and the NY Court of Appeals denied leave to appeal on October 21, 2025 — final; divestment has not been reversed. UNRESOLVED: whether trustees adopted the December 2024 proposal to exclude future private-market midstream/downstream fossil-fuel investment, and the outcome of the June 30, 2025 asset-manager net-zero-plan deadline. Note the office has changed hands — this work is Comptroller Brad Lander's; Mark Levine is the current Comptroller.

social.comparisonNote: Petaluma's own data.js lists a 6.5% poverty rate (2024, ACS) and a 0.44 Gini coefficient (2019) — figures that would represent enormous success by NYC standards. NYC's citywide Gini is 0.5563 (2024), the second-highest among large U.S. cities, with Manhattan alone at 0.5944, and 61.8% of New Yorkers fall short of the city's own True Cost of Living threshold (46% of working-age households on the independent FCNY measure) against Petaluma's much narrower affordability strain (34% cost-burdened on housing). The scale and mechanism also differ qualitatively: Petaluma has no equivalent to NYC's finance-sector wealth concentration (a $246,900 average Wall Street bonus for 2025 against Petaluma's local median incomes) or to a roughly 412,000-person undocumented workforce excluded from unemployment insurance. Note that the two portraits are NOT measuring the same thing when they both say 'poverty': Petaluma's 6.5% is the federal poverty rate, whose NYC equivalent is 18.0% (2024) — the 61.8% figure is a self-sufficiency threshold and must not be compared to it directly.
dataGaps: No NYC-specific dollar estimate for remittances sent abroad from the city could be located. This is the most on-dimension global-social flow for income & work and its absence is why the global lens leans on the finance channel. The NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs (MOIA) or the Center for Migration Studies of New York (CMSNY) would be the most likely holders of city-scale remittance modeling.

The headline TCOL Measure is built on 2018 ACS data projected to 2022, published in 2026. No post-2022 vintage of the official measure exists yet, so the dimension cannot say what the official rate is today — and the independent FCNY series suggests conditions improved somewhat between 2021 and 2024. MOERJ and the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity should be asked for the update cadence the Charter's annual-reporting mandate implies.

The official 'NYCgov Poverty Measure' (Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity / NYC Opportunity) publishes on a multi-year lag and no current-year percentage could be located from NYC Opportunity itself; its Poverty Research Team would have the authoritative current figure and could clarify how the NYCgov measure relates to the new TCOL measure.

No current, city-specific wage-theft dollar total was found. The widely-cited '$20 million/week' figure traces to former Manhattan DA Cyrus Vance (pre-2022) and is stale — the NYC Comptroller's Bureau of Labor Law or NYS DOL's Division of Labor Standards would hold current recovery totals.

Garment and retail global sourcing labour conditions specific to NYC-headquartered or NYC-based retailers were not quantified. NYC Economic Development Corporation (garment district initiatives) or the Worker Rights Consortium would be better positioned.

No single-vintage five-borough median household income table was assembled; the citywide 2024 ACS figure is used instead. Borough-level ACS income tables exist in the Rent Guidelines Board study appendices and should be extracted directly.

Estimates of NYC's undocumented population are ACS-modelled and range widely by method and year (~412,000 per MOIA for 2022, ~476,000 per the NYC Comptroller for 2019, ~611,000 in 2012). Note explicitly that Center for Migration Studies figures in the 600,000-670,000 range are NEW YORK STATE, not the city, and must not be substituted.

social.name: housing
social.levelRationale: Anchored on the headline: a 1.41% net rental vacancy rate against the 5% threshold in NY State's Emergency Tenant Protection Act, the statutory test for whether a 'housing emergency' exists (a LOWER rate means a WORSE emergency, and rent stabilization for ~996,600 units is sustained precisely because the market fails this test). At 3.5x below the line -- and 0.39% in the bottom rent quartile, meaning the affordable segment is functionally at zero -- the headline alone rules out anything at or below 'critical'. Adjusted UP by four material, well-sourced sub-indicators: (1) homelessness at an all-time record and still rising -- 194,531 unique individuals used DHS shelter during 2025, the most in system history, with ~96,500 people in shelter nightly in April 2026 and >350,000 New Yorkers without homes at 1 Jan 2026 -- reached AFTER the asylum-seeker population fell 51% from its Jan-2024 peak, so this is a structurally domestic record, not a migration shock; (2) the Right to Counsel collapse, from 71% of eligible tenants represented in Q4 FY2021 to 42% in Q4 FY2024 and 30% by March 2025, and 81% to 31% in the Bronx; (3) NYCHA's $78.3B twenty-year capital backlog, up 73% since 2017, with 633,808 households having applied for 200,000 Section 8 waitlist slots; (4) 86% of renter households earning under $25,000 outside means-tested housing severely rent burdened. Adjusted DOWN, and this is the reason the score is not 150: the citywide median rent-to-income ratio FELL from 34.3% to 29.5%, which NYCHVS calls the first decline since 2002, and NYCHVS's own conclusion is that 'the overall prevalence of rent burden in New York City declined for the first time in several survey cycles'; eviction filings fell 9.6% in 2024 and remain below pre-pandemic levels; and 2024-2026 delivered an unusually dense run of real instruments (City of Yes at 82,000 projected homes, Good Cause Eviction, 485-x, Local Law 126 of 2024, the 2026 rent freeze, the enacted pied-a-terre tax). Note also that the 4.54% 2021 comparator is described by NYCHVS itself as 'historically high', so the fall to 1.41% is reversion to and past NYC's chronic sub-3.5% norm rather than a new cliff. 135 therefore places housing as the most severe dimension in this portrait, clearly above 'critical', and just short of the scale ceiling -- with the measured improvement in median rent burden as the single named reason it is not 150.
social.indicator: Net rental vacancy rate (NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey), with rent burden and shelter census as co-headline indicators
social.value: 2.33% net rental vacancy rate (2023, 90% CI 1.72%-2.94%); 10.01% in 2021 -- the highest borough rate in both years
social.target: NY State Emergency Tenant Protection Act: a rental vacancy rate at or above 5% is the legal standard under which NYC could be found to no longer have a 'housing emergency' justifying rent stabilization; the city has been below this line at every survey and is now at less than a third of it. NYCHVS is conducted roughly every 3 years; the 2026 cycle is in the field (City of New York with the University of Michigan Survey Research Center, using CUNY students as field interviewers) with no published release date, so no post-City-of-Yes, post-rent-freeze measurement exists yet.
social.context:
Manhattan: 2.33% net rental vacancy rate (2023, 90% CI 1.72%-2.94%); 10.01% in 2021 -- the highest borough rate in both years

Citywide for comparison: 1.41% net rental vacancy rate citywide (2023 NYCHVS) -- 33,210 units available for rent out of a total stock of 2,357,000 occupied-plus-vacant-available rental units -- down from 4.54% in 2021, which NYCHVS itself describes as historically high. HPD calls 1.41% the lowest this measurement has been since the 1968 NYCHVS; the NYCHVS report, which has run since 1965, describes it as 'one of the lowest net rental vacancy rates on record'. For units renting under $1,100/month (the bottom rent quartile) the rate was 0.39%; second quartile 0.91%, third 0.78%, top quartile ($2,400+) 3.39%. On affordability the picture is genuinely mixed: the citywide median renter household paid 29.5% of income toward rent in 2023, down from 34.3% in 2021 -- the first decline since 2002, driven by income growth outpacing a 9% median rent increase against ~10% inflation -- but for renter households earning under $70,000 (the median renter income) the typical rent-to-income ratio was 54.0%, i.e. the typical below-median renter is severely rent burdened; and 86% of renter households earning under $25,000 outside means-tested housing were severely rent burdened. On the ACS basis (Furman Center) just over half of NYC renter households were rent burdened in 2023, 28.9% severely and 23.0% moderately. Homelessness is at an all-time high and rising: 87,442 people slept in DHS+HPD shelters in May 2026 (up from 73,219 in Dec 2024 and 65,640 in Dec 2023), ~96,500 people were in NYC shelters nightly in April 2026 including 30,955 children, a record 194,531 unique individuals used the DHS system over the course of 2025, and Coalition for the Homeless counts >350,000 New Yorkers without homes as of 1 Jan 2026 -- all reached while the separate asylum-seeker shelter population fell from a Jan-2024 peak of ~70,000 to ~33,300 (Sept 2025).

NYC's housing crisis differs from a small city's in that market failure is legally instrumentalized: the ultra-low vacancy rate is not just a symptom but the statutory mechanism that keeps the ~996,600-unit rent-stabilization system (27% of the overall housing stock, 41% of rental units) in place, which in turn shapes state and city legislative fights every few years. A small city like Petaluma has no equivalent regulatory apparatus keyed to vacancy. The scale of shortage -- 33,210 available units against 3,432,000 occupied households -- points to underproduction as the core lever: occupied households grew by 275,000 (+9%) between 2021 and 2023 while the total housing stock grew by only 61,000 units (3,644,000 to 3,705,000). Caveats: the 2023 NYCHVS is a sample survey (fielded January to mid-June 2023) whose margins of error widen sharply at the borough level for a metric already near zero -- NYCHVS states that borough rates and rates by type of rental housing are all statistically similar to one another; and current conditions are not yet independently re-measured. The two directions of travel in this dimension must be read together rather than averaged: supply scarcity and homelessness are at or near record-bad levels while median rent burden and eviction filings improved.
actions: Know your rights under Good Cause Eviction and, if facing eviction, contact Right to Counsel NYC Coalition or Housing Court Answers for same-day help finding a Right to Counsel-eligible attorney -- and know that citywide representation has fallen to roughly 30%, so asking for an adjournment to secure counsel matters.

Apply for NYCHA public housing and Section 8 waitlists when open (watch nyc.gov/nycha for the next application window) and report HPD violations (heat, hot water, mold, pests) via 311 or NYC's HPDOnline portal to build the legal record landlords are held to.

Support or join a tenant association -- Met Council on Housing, Right to Counsel NYC Coalition, and Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development (ANHD) all organize building- and borough-level tenant power, especially in the Bronx where eviction filing rates are more than double every other borough's.

Weigh in on City of Yes-enabled rezonings and City Planning Commission/Community Board hearings in your neighborhood -- local implementation (ADUs, small-building conversions) is where the 82,000-unit citywide projection will be won or lost building by building.

If you are a basement-apartment tenant or landlord, track the DOB/HPD legalization pilot rulemaking under Local Law 126 of 2024 (public comment periods via nyc.gov) -- applications close 20 April 2029, and properties in flood-prone areas are categorically excluded.

Check whether your landlord is on the Public Advocate's Worst Landlord Watchlist (landlordwatchlist.com) before renewing or signing a lease, and report unresolved conditions to help build enforcement pressure.

subIndicators.name: DHS/HPD shelter census and record system-wide use

subIndicators.name: NYCHA scale and capital need
subIndicators.value: NYCHA provides housing to 511,384 authorized residents in over 177,565 apartments across 335 developments, through conventional public housing, Section 8 and PACT/RAD combined (Fact Sheet, released January 2025). Components: 298,206 residents in 152,926 apartments across 243 developments in conventional public housing (Section 9); 46,455 residents in 24,639 apartments across 92 developments converted under PACT/RAD; 107,979 families (223,114 authorized residents) assisted through Section 8. NYCHA public housing and Section 8 together occupy 10.9% of the city's rental apartments and house 6.2% of NYC's population; average public-housing family income is $26,129 and average monthly rent $621. The 2023 Physical Needs Assessment found $78.3B in 20-year capital repair needs across the 264 directly-managed properties (161,400 apartments), up 73% from $45.3B in the 2017 PNA, with $57.8B (74%) in apartments, heating systems, building exteriors and plumbing; the next PNA is slated for 2028, and NYCHA's Jan-2025 Fact Sheet characterises the backlog as 'nearly $80 billion'. NYCHA's Section 8 voucher waitlist reopened in June 2024 for the first time since 10 Dec 2009: 633,808 households applied, of which 200,000 were selected by lottery.
subIndicators.source: NYCHA Fact Sheet (released January 2025); NYCHA 2023 Physical Needs Assessment; NYCHA press release 2024-08-01

subIndicators.name: Rent-stabilized stock and Rent Guidelines Board action
subIndicators.value: 996,600 rent-stabilized units in 2023 -- 27% of NYC's overall housing stock and 41% of all rental units, of which about 76% (758,700 units) are stabilized via the Emergency Tenant Protection Act. subIndicators.name: Right to Counsel representation rate, citywide and Bronx
subIndicators.value: Attorney representation for eligible tenants facing eviction fell from 71% (Q4 FY2021) to 42% (Q4 FY2024) citywide, and further to 30% by March 2025. In the Bronx, where evictions are most concentrated, representation fell from 81% (Q4 2021) to 31% (Q4 2024). The full-representation caseload providers were expected to carry grew 51% from FY2019 to FY2024 (approximately 16,300 to 24,500 households), while demand for brief legal services grew 475% over the same period. Where full representation was secured, 89% of tenants remained stably housed (FY2024); across 2018-2023, 81% of represented households avoided eviction (34,571 of 41,161 cases). Providers estimate the City would need to more than double its spending to meet demand; advocates have called for $350M annually.
subIndicators.source: NYC Comptroller, 'Evictions Up, Representation Down' (May 2025)

subIndicators.name: Illegal/basement apartments and Hurricane Ida
subIndicators.value: 11 of the 13 Hurricane Ida-related deaths in NYC (1 Sept 2021) were drownings in basement apartments, mostly of immigrants; DOB found 5 of the 6 apartments where deaths occurred were illegally converted. Against an estimated 100,000+ illegal basement/cellar units citywide, the legalization record is close to nil: the Basement Apartment Conversion Pilot Program (BACPP), launched in 2019 in Brooklyn Community District 5, drew just 5 active participants out of roughly 8,000 homeowners contacted, against an initial goal of 40 units, and NO participant had completed a conversion as of mid-2025 -- blocked by the State Multiple Dwelling Law, accessibility mandates, cost and unforeseen physical non-compliances. A new citywide pilot mandated by Local Law 126 of 2024 (part of City of Yes for Housing Opportunity) is the current pathway: DOB/HPD published proposed rules in November 2025, eligibility is limited to apartments that existed before 20 April 2024 in named community districts with basic safety features, owners have until 20 April 2029 to apply and 10 years to reach full compliance. Critically, properties in flood-prone areas are categorically ineligible -- excluding the very exposure that killed 11 people in 2021.
subIndicators.source: ABC News and NBC New York coverage of Ida deaths and DOB findings; CHPC, Basement Apartment Conversion Pilot Program Final Report; NYC HPD/DOB press release 074-25 on the Local Law 126 of 2024 pilot rules

subIndicators.name: Housing quality: HPD violations and Worst Landlord Watchlist

subIndicators.name: 485-x and Good Cause Eviction, statewide adoption
subIndicators.value: 485-x ('Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers') replaced the expired 421-a tax incentive, adopted 20 April 2024, requiring permanently affordable units on a sliding scale: 25% at a weighted average 80% AMI for rental projects of 100+ units (35-year benefit), 25% at 60% AMI for very large projects of 150+ units in Zones A/B (40-year benefit), 20% at 80% AMI for projects of 6-99 units (35-year benefit), with restricted units permanently rent stabilized and construction wage floors from $40/hour up to $72.45/hour by zone and project size. Good Cause Eviction took effect 20 April 2024 in NYC by default (rent-increase caps and just-cause eviction protections for most market-rate tenants below roughly 345% of Fair Market Rent); 17 NY municipalities have since opted in, and approximately 1 million renters statewide are now covered.
subIndicators.source: NYC HPD 485-x program page; NY State Senate press release on Good Cause adoption

global.levelRationale: Scored on the two things that are actually quantified plus the direction of policy. MAGNITUDE (pulls the score down from 'critical'): the primary, published measure of housing withheld from the market -- units held for seasonal, recreational or occasional use, the NYCHVS category that contains pieds-a-terre and dedicated short-term rentals -- is 58,810 units in 2023, about 1.6% of a 3,705,000-unit stock, and it FELL 43% from 102,900 in 2021 (74,950 in 2017). The State's own estimate of units above the new pied-a-terre tax thresholds is ~14,000, with a DOF-derived Comptroller sample of 19,107 properties of which 17,125 are in Manhattan. Blackstone and Ivanhoe Cambridge hold 11,200 units at Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village. Those are real transmission-channel quantities, and they are modest and shrinking. TRANSPARENCY (pulls the score up): the anti-anonymity regime has been dismantled at both federal and state level within 12 months -- FinCEN's March-2025 interim final rule removed roughly 99.8% of entities from Corporate Transparency Act beneficial-ownership reporting by exempting all US-formed entities; the residential real estate GTOs expired 28 Feb 2026; their nationwide replacement rule took effect 1 March 2026 and was vacated by the U.S. District Court for E.D. Texas on 19 March 2026 (on appeal), so no federal shell-company residential reporting requirement is in force; and New York's own LLC Transparency Act, effective 1 Jan 2026, was narrowed by the Governor's 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432 to reach only non-US-formed LLCs, so the state does not backstop the federal gap. That is the weakest disclosure posture since the GTOs began in 2016. COUNTERWEIGHT: New York State enacted a pied-a-terre surcharge on 26 May 2026, effective 1 July 2026 -- the first binding fiscal instrument against non-primary-residence ownership after roughly seven years of failed proposals. Net: a real and worsening opacity problem attached to a measured channel of modest and declining magnitude, with a new tool just switched on. 60 -- above 'needs attention', clearly short of 'critical'. The previous level of 100 rested on an unverifiable '~10% of Manhattan condo transactions' figure that has been removed, and cannot be sustained without it. Confidence medium: the transparency findings are firm, the magnitude figures are firm, but no source quantifies the share of NYC purchases made by foreign nationals or anonymous entities.
global.indicator: NYC housing withheld from the market for non-primary-residence and occasional use, and the visibility of global and anonymous capital in NYC housing
global.value: PRIMARY QUANTIFICATION: 58,810 NYC housing units were held for seasonal, recreational or occasional use in 2023 -- 26% of all units vacant but not available for rent or sale, the single largest such category -- down from 102,900 in 2021 and 74,950 in 2017 (2023 NYCHVS). New York State enacted a pied-a-terre surcharge on 26 May 2026 in the FY2026-27 Budget Bill, effective 1 July 2026 and sunsetting 30 June 2031, taxing non-primary residences at 4.0-6.5% for Class 2 condos and co-ops above $1M and 0.8-1.3% for Class 1 homes above $5M in Phase 1; the State estimates ~14,000 NYC apartments and homes fall in scope, and the Comptroller's DOF-based analysis identified 19,107 properties of which 17,125 are in Manhattan, with revenue revised to $340-380M from an initial $500M. TRANSPARENCY REGIME, as of July 2026: FinCEN's residential real estate Geographic Targeting Orders -- which required title insurers to identify the natural persons behind shell-company, non-financed purchases over $300,000 in covered metros including NYC -- were last renewed effective 10 Oct 2025 and expired 28 Feb 2026. Their nationwide replacement, the Residential Real Estate Rule (finalized Aug 2024, delayed from 1 Dec 2025), took effect 1 March 2026 and was VACATED by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas on 19 March 2026; FinCEN states reporting persons need not file and face no liability for not filing, and FinCEN and DOJ have appealed. Separately, FinCEN's interim final rule of 21 March 2025 (effective 26 March 2025) exempted all US-formed entities -- including the LLCs typically used to hold anonymous NYC real estate -- from Corporate Transparency Act beneficial-ownership reporting, removing roughly 99.8% of originally covered entities; a final rule reached OIRA on 5 June 2026 and remains unpublished. New York's own LLC Transparency Act took effect 1 Jan 2026 but, after the Governor's 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432, reaches only LLCs formed outside the United States, exempting domestic LLCs. INSTITUTIONAL OWNERSHIP: Blackstone (headquartered in Manhattan) and Ivanhoe Cambridge -- a subsidiary of Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec, a Quebec public pension fund -- have owned Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village (11,200 apartments, ~30,000 residents) since closing a $5.3B purchase in December 2015; the complex is referenced in the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Housing's 22 March 2019 letter to Blackstone's CEO, co-signed by the chair-rapporteur of the UN Working Group on Business and Human Rights, which followed Leilani Farha's 2017 Human Rights Council report on the financialization of housing (A/HRC/34/51). GLOBAL PROPORTION: UN-Habitat's World Cities Report 2026, 'The Global Housing Crisis: Pathways to Action' (launched at WUF13, Baku, May 2026), finds 1.13 billion people living in informal settlements and slums in 2024, up from 895 million in 2000, and approximately 3.4 billion lacking access to secure, safe and adequate housing -- a reminder that NYC's crisis, however severe, is a crisis of price, scarcity and regulation within a fully formal, serviced housing stock, categorically different from the absence of durable shelter facing over a billion people.
global.target: No binding NYC or US target exists for foreign or anonymous capital flows into housing. The relevant global-framework anchor is the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Housing's call (since 2017, A/HRC/34/51) for states to ensure housing markets serve human need rather than investment returns. Instruments now in force or in litigation: the NYS pied-a-terre surcharge (enacted 26 May 2026, effective 1 July 2026 -- the first binding NYC-applicable instrument in this space); FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Rule (vacated 19 March 2026, on appeal); the federal Corporate Transparency Act (narrowed March 2025 to foreign-formed entities only); and NY State's LLC Transparency Act (effective 1 Jan 2026, narrowed to non-US-formed LLCs after the 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432).
global.context: The transmission channel is financial, not physical: global capital reaches NYC housing through shell-company purchases of luxury condos, institutional acquisition of rent-regulated portfolios financed partly through global pension and sovereign capital (as with Ivanhoe Cambridge/CDPQ's stake in Stuyvesant Town), and NYC-headquartered private-equity firms' single-family-rental strategies elsewhere in the US and abroad. This belongs in the Doughnut's global-social lens because it is the mirror image of NYC's local scarcity: the same undersupplied, high-value stock that burdens NYC renters is an attractive store of value for capital raised anywhere. Two honest qualifications. First, the measured magnitude is modest and falling -- 58,810 withheld units is 1.6% of the stock and 43% below 2021 -- so this channel is a real but second-order driver of the 1.41% vacancy rate compared with underproduction. Second, this lens quantifies capital flowing INTO NYC rather than NYC's effect on people elsewhere; it is a transmission-channel reading of R2 rather than an embodied-footprint reading, and no source quantifies the share of NYC purchases made by foreign nationals or anonymous entities. What has changed decisively is visibility: between March 2025 and March 2026 the federal and New York State disclosure regimes were both narrowed to exempt domestic entities and the nationwide residential reporting rule was vacated, leaving the flow less measurable than at any point since 2016 -- at the same moment New York finally enacted a tax on it. A small city like Petaluma has no comparable exposure to global capital markets in its housing stock.
global.source: NYC HPD 2023 NYCHVS (seasonal/occasional-use units); NYS FY2026-27 Budget Bill pied-a-terre provisions as analysed by Holland & Knight; FinCEN news releases, RRE newsroom and Federal Register notices; NY Department of State LLC Transparency Act guidance; OHCHR Special Rapporteur reports and correspondence; UN-Habitat World Cities Report 2026

policyAnchors.name: Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA) of 2019
policyAnchors.relevance: State law that closed vacancy decontrol and capped preferential-rent and individual/major capital improvement rent increases; NYCHVS confirms that 'legislation enacted in 2019 limited the circumstances under which housing units could exit rent stabilization', underpinning the current 996,600-unit stabilized stock whose size and vacancy dynamics are central to this dossier.
policyAnchors.status: Remains in force; repeatedly cited alongside HVS vacancy math as a reason institutional owners including Blackstone have described profitability pressure on regulated portfolios such as Stuyvesant Town. Not independently re-verified for 2026 amendments in this review pass.

policyAnchors.name: Good Cause Eviction Law (NY State, 2024)
policyAnchors.relevance: Extends just-cause eviction and rent-increase-cap protections to a large share of NYC's previously-unprotected market-rate renters.
policyAnchors.status: In effect since 20 April 2024 in NYC by default; 17 municipalities statewide have since opted in, with approximately 1 million renters covered statewide as of 2025.

policyAnchors.name: 485-x (Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers)
policyAnchors.relevance: Replacement for the expired 421-a tax incentive; ties new-construction tax exemptions to permanent affordability requirements (20-25% of units at a 60-80% AMI weighted average by project tier), permanent rent stabilization of restricted units, construction wage floors and MWBE contracting goals.
policyAnchors.status: Adopted 20 April 2024; construction must commence between 15 June 2022 and 15 June 2034 and complete by 15 June 2038. Existing 421-a(16) projects have an extended completion deadline if they do not convert.

policyAnchors.name: City of Yes for Housing Opportunity
policyAnchors.relevance: Citywide zoning overhaul intended to legalize more housing types (ADUs, small apartment buildings, office conversions) and reduce parking mandates; includes the Universal Affordability Preference (20% density bonus for permanently affordable space) and mandated the Local Law 126 of 2024 basement legalization pilot.
policyAnchors.status: Adopted by City Council 5 December 2024, with a projected 82,000 new homes over 15 years and $5B in accompanying City/State infrastructure funding secured in the Council negotiation. Advocates and researchers argue this falls well short of the scale implied by the 275,000-household growth NYC absorbed between 2021 and 2023 against total housing-stock growth of only 61,000 units.

policyAnchors.name: Fair Housing Framework -- Local Law 167 of 2023 -- and Where We Live NYC
policyAnchors.relevance: Codifies NYC's commitment to affirmatively furthering fair housing; requires HPD and DCP to produce a citywide fair housing assessment and plan every five years, with five-year housing production targets for each community district and a strategic equity framework. Where We Live NYC is the resulting fair-housing plan.
policyAnchors.status: ADJUDICATED IN REVIEW: the Fair Housing Framework is Local Law 167 of 2023 (Int. 1031-2023 / Int. 1031-A), 'A Local Law to amend the New York city charter, in relation to a fair housing plan, and to repeal local law number 133 for the year 2018' -- passed by the Council 15 Nov 2023 and signed by Mayor Adams 13 Dec 2023. The 'LL 174 of 2021' citation that appeared in the research brief is not a real law: the 2021 local laws run 1 through 173, and Local Law 174 of 2017 is the unrelated citywide agency equity-assessment law. 'Where We Live NYC 2025', the city's second five-year fair housing plan, was finalized in 2025.

policyAnchors.name: Right to Counsel (NYC Local Law 136 of 2017; expanded citywide by Local Law 54 of 2021)
policyAnchors.relevance: Guarantees free legal representation to income-eligible tenants facing eviction in Housing Court and NYCHA tenancy-termination proceedings; the single biggest lever shown to keep tenants stably housed (89% remained stably housed with full representation in FY2024).
policyAnchors.status: In effect citywide, but chronically underfunded relative to a full-representation caseload that grew 51% from FY2019 to FY2024 and brief-services demand that grew 475%. Representation fell from 71% (Q4 FY2021) to 42% (Q4 FY2024) and to 30% by March 2025 citywide, and from 81% to 31% in the Bronx, per the NYC Comptroller's May 2025 report. Signed as Int. 214-B on 11 August 2017.

policyAnchors.name: NYCHA PACT/RAD and the Public Housing Preservation Trust
policyAnchors.relevance: Mechanisms for routing private and federal (Section 8/RAD) capital into NYCHA's $78.3B, 20-year physical needs backlog without full privatization.
policyAnchors.status: PACT/RAD conversions continue: 92 developments and 24,639 apartments housing 46,455 authorized residents converted as of the January-2025 Fact Sheet. The Public Housing Preservation Trust (created 2022) provides an additional financing vehicle. The 2023 PNA remains the assessment of record with the next PNA slated for 2028. Not independently re-verified for a mid-2026 status update -- flagged as a data gap.

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 126 of 2024 -- basement and cellar apartment legalization pilot
policyAnchors.relevance: The current legal pathway for the estimated 100,000+ illegally occupied basement and cellar units citywide, mandated by City of Yes for Housing Opportunity; the direct policy response to the 11 basement drowning deaths in Hurricane Ida.
policyAnchors.status: DOB and HPD published proposed rules in November 2025. Eligibility is limited to apartments that existed before 20 April 2024, in community districts named in the law, with basic safety features (smoke and gas alarms, central heating, adequate egress, boiler separation). Owners have until 20 April 2029 to apply and 10 years to reach full compliance. Properties in flood-prone areas are categorically ineligible -- excluding the exposure that caused the 2021 deaths. Its predecessor, the 2019 BACPP pilot in Brooklyn CD5, completed zero conversions.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Rent Guidelines Board 2026-27 rent freeze
policyAnchors.relevance: First-ever freeze applied to both 1-year and 2-year rent-stabilized lease renewals; a direct, near-term test of Mayor Mamdani's affordability agenda given the RGB's role as sole regulator of rents on 996,600 units.
policyAnchors.status: Approved 7-1 by the RGB on 25 June 2026; 0% increase for both lease lengths effective 1 Oct 2026 to 30 Sept 2027. A pro-landlord board member resigned in protest hours before the vote. Landlord groups and some housing economists argue the freeze does not address underlying vacancy/supply scarcity and could reduce maintenance investment; tenant advocates frame it as immediate relief for burdened renters.

policyAnchors.name: NYS pied-a-terre surcharge (FY2026-27 Budget Bill)
policyAnchors.relevance: The first binding fiscal instrument aimed at non-primary-residence ownership of NYC housing, after roughly seven years of failed proposals; directly addresses the global-lens channel of housing held as a store of value rather than a home.
policyAnchors.status: Enacted 26 May 2026 as part of the NYS FY2026-27 Budget Bill; effective 1 July 2026 with a component retroactive to 1 January 2026; sunsets 30 June 2031 unless extended. Phase 1 (to 30 June 2028): Class 2 condos and co-ops above $1M taxed at 4.0% / 5.25% / 6.5% by bracket; Class 1 homes above $5M at 0.8% / 1.05% / 1.3%. Phase 2 (2028-2031) applies a $5M threshold across all classes. An estimated ~14,000 NYC units are in scope; the Comptroller has revised expected revenue to $340-380M from an initial $500M.

social.comparisonNote: Petaluma's housing entry (data.js, level 60) reports 34% cost-burdened households and 214 unhoused persons (point-in-time count, 2024) against a target of <30% burdened and zero unhoused -- serious for a city of ~60,000, but a single-order-of-magnitude problem measured with a straightforward annual PIT count. NYC's housing crisis is legally structural rather than simply a burden rate: a 1.41% vacancy rate is itself the statutory trigger sustaining rent stabilization for 996,600 units. NYC is also worse on the burden metric, not merely bigger -- just over half of NYC renter households are rent-burdened on the ACS basis against Petaluma's 34%, with 28.9% severely burdened -- and at 8.3M people the affected population is roughly two orders of magnitude larger. NYC's shelter system alone served 194,531 unique people in 2025, roughly 900x Petaluma's entire PIT unhoused count and about 2.3% of NYC's population passing through DHS shelter in a single year, with more than 350,000 New Yorkers without homes at the start of 2026. NYC also carries two housing dimensions Petaluma has no equivalent of: a $78.3B public-housing capital backlog (NYCHA, 511,384 residents) and a global-capital dynamic -- anonymous-LLC and non-primary-residence ownership, private-equity ownership of regulated stock -- that a small inland city simply is not exposed to. The one respect in which NYC is moving faster than Petaluma is policy: City of Yes, Good Cause Eviction, 485-x, a rent freeze and an enacted pied-a-terre tax all landed within 26 months.
dataGaps: No official combined point-in-time shelter total exists. The DHS/HPD census (Coalition for the Homeless) and the asylum-seeker-specific census (NYC Comptroller) are separately maintained series on different definitions, and summing them would produce a derived figure presented where a published one is expected. This dossier therefore reports the two components separately and attributes each; no combined total appears anywhere in it, and none should be introduced. The DHS Daily Report dataset on NYC Open Data is the route to an authoritative combined daily figure and should be pulled in Phase 2.

Staten Island's 2023 net rental vacancy rate is not reported in the NYCHVS because too few vacant-and-available units were sampled there for a reliable estimate. This is a sampling-reliability suppression rather than a Census disclosure-avoidance suppression, so restricted-use NYCHVS microdata would not necessarily yield a usable figure either; a defensible Staten Island vacancy rate may simply not be estimable from this survey.

No source quantifies the share of NYC residential purchases made by foreign nationals or by anonymous entities. The dossier's earlier '~10% of Manhattan condo transactions are pied-a-terre per NYC DOF data' claim was removed in review as unverifiable -- the only '10%' figure that could be sourced is DOF's Class 2 assessment ratio, an unrelated statistic. The NYCHVS seasonal/occasional-use count (58,810) and the pied-a-terre tax's ~14,000-unit scope estimate are the best available primary proxies, and neither measures purchaser nationality or ownership anonymity. NYC DOF's pied-a-terre tax administration data, once a filing year is complete, would be the first direct source.

HPD housing-code violation counts and heat/hot-water complaint volumes by borough (as opposed to by individual landlord/building, which the Worst Landlord Watchlist covers) were not retrieved; NYC Open Data's 'Housing Maintenance Code Violations' dataset would have this.

NYU Furman Center's State of Renters and Their Homes 2024 returns 403 Forbidden to direct fetch on both www and non-www domains. All Furman-derived figures in this dossier -- borough severe rent burden, borough and community-district eviction filing rates, the citywide ACS burden shares -- were recovered from search indexing rather than the report itself and are held at medium confidence. The Staten Island severe-rent-burden figure (32.1%) specifically was not recoverable on re-verification. The NYC Comptroller's Asylum Seeker Census page also returns 403. Both should be obtained directly in Phase 2.

The dimension is anchored on a survey fielded January-June 2023. Every headline figure predates City of Yes, Good Cause Eviction, 485-x and the 2026 rent freeze. The 2026 NYCHVS is in the field (City of New York with the University of Michigan Survey Research Center, CUNY students as field interviewers) with no announced release date; the dimension will need re-scoring on publication.

social.name: mobility
social.levelRationale: Anchored on the published headline: 20.6% of NYC workers drove alone to work (ACS 2024 1-Year, place-level), against the shared <50% threshold used in the Petaluma portrait. At 41% of the threshold this argues for roughly -85 on the headline alone. Moved up ~20 points under R1 for two material, independently verified structural failures inside the same dimension: (1) SUBWAY ACCESSIBILITY -- only 160 of 472 stations (33.9%) have stair-free access per MTA's own July 2026 count, leaving ~66% inaccessible, with the court-approved compliance horizon set at 2055; (2) BUS SPEEDS -- 8.17 mph citywide in 2024, DOWN 0.6% from 8.22 mph in 2015 and far short of the City's own 25%-improvement goal, with Manhattan at 6.29 mph. Also pulling up, though less: mean commute time of 40.6 minutes, among the longest of any large US city; Staten Island at 50.8% is the one borough above the threshold; Fair Fares enrolls only 41% of its ~940,000 eligible population; and NYC DOT has missed its Local Law 195 bus- and bike-lane mileage mandates every recent year. NOT moved further up, for three reasons independently verified in adversarial review: (a) TRAFFIC SAFETY IS A STRENGTH, NOT A SHORTFALL -- 2025 recorded 205 traffic deaths, the fewest since record-keeping began in 1910, down 19% year-on-year and 31% since Vision Zero launched in 2014, with Q1 2026 the third-lowest on record; an earlier version of this rationale asserted fatalities were at post-Vision-Zero highs, which primary NYC DOT sources refute; (b) the Fair Fares gap is smaller than previously stated (41% of ~940,000, not 37% of 1.4M) and is closing, with the income ceiling raised to 150% FPL and a further expansion to 200% FPL agreed in June 2026; (c) congestion pricing is operating, legally secure following Judge Liman's final ruling of 3 March 2026 in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy, and delivering measured reductions (11% fewer vehicle entries, 27 million fewer entries in year one). Per R5, a strongly negative level is the correct and honest result for NYC mobility mode share and has not been nudged toward zero.
social.indicator: Percent of workers 16+ who drove alone to work
social.value: 5.2% drove alone (47,452 of 914,910 workers 16+); mean travel time to work 31.4 min (+-0.6) -- shortest of the 5 boroughs. Also the highest work-from-home share (18.1%) and the highest walk share (18.3%).
social.target: No official NYC target exists for this exact metric; using the same informal <50% drive-alone threshold applied in the Petaluma portrait for direct comparability (R4). NYC's own binding mode-shift commitments are structural rather than numeric (NYC Streets Plan / Local Law 195 of 2019 mandates minimum annual bus- and bike-lane mileage; City of Yes and PlaNYC 2023 set car-lite land-use and TOD goals).
social.context:
Manhattan: 5.2% drove alone (47,452 of 914,910 workers 16+); mean travel time to work 31.4 min (+-0.6) -- shortest of the 5 boroughs. Also the highest work-from-home share (18.1%) and the highest walk share (18.3%).

Citywide for comparison: 20.6% citywide (840,263 of 4,070,607 workers 16+) drove alone in 2024 -- the officially published figure for the Census place 'New York city, New York'. Full published mode share: 48.7% public transportation, 12.5% worked from home, 9.6% walked, 4.4% carpooled, 1.7% bicycle, 1.2% other, 1.1% taxicab, 0.2% motorcycle. Only 25.1% of workers used a car, truck or van at all. DENOMINATOR NOTE: the ACS universe for this table is all workers 16+ INCLUDING those who worked from home, which is the same basis as Petaluma's 72.6% and therefore the correct comparison. If the work-from-home population is excluded from the denominator (i.e. mode share among people who actually travel to work), drove-alone rises to 23.6% (840,263 of 3,560,755). Both figures are stated because the 12.5% work-from-home share materially affects the percentage. By borough, drove-alone ranges from 5.2% in Manhattan to 50.8% in Staten Island -- a ~46-point spread within one city.

This is the dimension where NYC and Petaluma diverge most sharply: Petaluma's 72.6% drive-alone rate vs. NYC's 20.6% reflects two fundamentally different built environments -- a car-dependent small city vs. a transit-first megacity with the country's only 24/7 subway system. But a low drive-alone rate does not mean NYC's mobility system is healthy. Two failures are severe and well-evidenced: only about a third of subway stations (160 of 472) offer stair-free access, with the court-approved compliance horizon at 2055; and bus speeds have not improved in a decade, running at 8.17 mph citywide and 6.29 mph in Manhattan against the City's own goal of a 25% improvement. Mean commute time, 40.6 minutes, is among the longest of any large US city. Traffic safety, by contrast, is now a genuine strength: 2025 was the safest year in recorded NYC history (205 deaths, down 31% since Vision Zero began in 2014), and the first quarter of 2026 was the third-safest on record. The policy lever with the most momentum is congestion pricing (Central Business District Tolling Program), which is reshaping the denominator itself by pulling trips out of cars, and which survived the federal attempt to terminate it with a final court ruling in the MTA's favour in March 2026. NOTE on a claim removed in review: the widely-repeated assertion that NYC buses are 'the slowest of any major US city' is not supported by the NYC Comptroller report usually cited for it and could not be sourced to a primary comparative dataset, so it is not asserted here; what the source does support is a decade of stagnation against the City's own target.
social.source: US Census Bureau ACS 2024 1-Year, Tables B08301 and S0801, New York County, New York
actions: Apply for Fair Fares NYC through ACCESS HRA if household income is at or below 150% of the Federal Poverty Level (rising to 200% FPL in fall 2026) and you are aged 18-64 -- only about 41% of the ~940,000 currently eligible New Yorkers are enrolled (nyc.gov/site/hra/help/fair-fares.page).

Submit testimony or comment to NYC DOT / City Council on Streets Plan (LL195) compliance, since the agency has missed its statutory annual bus- and bike-lane mileage mandates every recent year measured.

Track and comment on the Interborough Express (IBX) scoping and environmental review through MTA's project page as it moves toward a Draft Environmental Impact Statement (mta.info/project/interborough-express).

Support or monitor the MTA subway accessibility capital program (2025-2029, $7.1B) -- the Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, lead plaintiff in the settlement, tracks compliance with the interim milestones; 160 of 472 stations are accessible today against a 2055 deadline.

Press for faster bus service through the MTA/DOT bus priority programme (busways, camera-enforced bus lanes, all-door boarding), since citywide bus speeds have not improved in a decade (8.17 mph in 2024 vs 8.22 in 2015) against the City's own 25%-improvement goal.
Use and provide feedback on Vision Zero infrastructure (20 mph zones under Sammy's Law, open streets, protected bike and bus lanes) via NYC DOT's public engagement channels (nyc.gov/visionzero).

Follow congestion pricing's toll-schedule developments (rising to $12 in 2028 and $15 in 2031) via MTA's Congestion Relief Zone page, and check eligibility for the Low-Income Discount Plan, which halves the peak toll from the 11th trip in a calendar month.
