social.boroughsNote: The five borough worker totals sum to exactly 4,070,607 and the five borough drove-alone counts to exactly 840,263 -- identical to the published place-level totals for New York city, New York. No borough figure is interpolated, pro-rated or derived; all five are published county estimates.
social.neighborhoodNote: Bay Terrace, Fresh Meadows, Glen Oaks and Oakland Gardens in northeastern/eastern Queens are documented transit deserts: no subway access, with residents dependent on express buses and the LIRR. A Streetsblog NYC op-ed (January 2020) on the Queens bus-network redesign named these neighborhoods specifically, noting the redesign would cut them from all-day, seven-day express bus service to weekday rush hours only, even though their lack of transit alternatives is what makes the express bus a lifeline. This contrasts with Manhattan's near-universal subway proximity (5.2% drive-alone, 51.0% transit). CAVEATS ADDED IN REVIEW: an earlier version attributed these neighborhoods to 'roughly Community District 11' -- they in fact span several different Queens community districts, so no single CD is named here. An earlier version also claimed 'fewer than 4 in 10 Queens residents overall can walk to a subway station'; that statistic could not be sourced and has been removed. The nearest sourceable figure is a citywide one (more than a third of all New Yorkers do not live within walking distance of a subway or rail station), which is a different measure at a different geography. A Queens-specific subway-walkshed percentage remains a dataGap.

subIndicators.name: Subway stations with ADA (stair-free) accessibility
subIndicators.value: 160 of 472 subway stations accessible (33.9%) as of July 2026 -- meaning roughly 66% of stations remain stair-inaccessible. MTA states this is 'nearly eleven times the 15 stations that were accessible when the ADA passed in 1990'. The Governor's office reported 154 accessible as of 31 December 2025 after 10 station accessibility projects completed during 2025, consistent with 160 by mid-2026. The 2022/2023 class-action settlement baseline was 364 inaccessible stations of 472, i.e. 108 accessible (~23%) at time of settlement.
subIndicators.source: MTA (primary), accessibility article updated 22 July 2026; MTA ADA Settlement Notice for the 2023 baseline; NY Governor's Office 31 December 2025 release for the 154 interim count
subIndicators.reviewNote: Upgraded from secondary reporting (HelpNewYork.com / amNewYork) to an MTA primary statement during adversarial review.

subIndicators.name: MTA subway/SIR accessibility settlement commitment
subIndicators.value: Settlement commits the MTA to making at least 95% of the 364 stations that were inaccessible at the time of settlement stair-free accessible by 2055 (equivalently ~454 of 472 stations, ~96% systemwide), via interim milestones: 81 stations already contracted in the 2020-2024 or prior capital plans, then +85 by 2035, +90 by 2045, +90 by 2055 (81+85+90+90 = 346 = 95% of 364). The MTA must dedicate no less than 14.69% of the NYC Transit portion of any capital plan of $35.389B or more to station accessibility, with a floor of 8%. Consolidated cases: Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, et al. v. MTA (NY State Supreme Court, No. 153765/2017) and De La Rosa, et al. v. MTA (S.D.N.Y., No. 19-cv-04406); fairness hearings scheduled April 2023.
subIndicators.source: MTA ADA Settlement Notice (primary)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Corrected in review: the 95% target applies to the 364 then-inaccessible stations, not to all 472 as previously stated. The milestone arithmetic (346 = 95% of 364) confirms the corrected base.

subIndicators.name: Mean travel time to work
subIndicators.value: 40.6 minutes (+-0.3) citywide -- among the longest of any large US city. By borough: Manhattan 31.4, Brooklyn 41.7, Bronx 43.3, Queens 43.8, Staten Island 45.4.
subIndicators.source: US Census Bureau, ACS 2024 1-Year Estimates, Subject Table S0801 (variable S0801_C01_046), place 'New York city, New York' -- officially published at city level
subIndicators.reviewNote: Replaced an author-derived worker-weighted estimate of ~40.4 minutes with the published place-level figure of 40.6, per R3. Manhattan corrected from 31.5 (+-0.4) to the published 31.4 (+-0.6).

subIndicators.name: Super-commuters (90+ minute one-way commute)
subIndicators.value: Staten Island (Richmond County) reported as having the 5th-highest super-commuter share of any US county at 14.3%; elevated super-commuting documented across the outer boroughs and concentrated among public-transit riders (14.0% of transit commuters vs. 2.4% of drivers).
subIndicators.source: Apartment List / Stacker analysis of Census commuting microdata (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary Census tabulation in this review)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Confidence lowered to low: this rests on a third-party analysis that was not re-fetched or confirmed against a primary Census table during adversarial review.

subIndicators.name: Average bus speed
subIndicators.value: 8.17 mph citywide in 2024 -- DOWN 0.6% from 8.22 mph in 2015 (8.06 in 2019), i.e. a decade of no improvement, and far short of the City's stated goal of improving bus speeds citywide by 25%. By borough (2024): Staten Island 12.6 mph, Queens 8.75, Bronx 7.65, Brooklyn 7.37, Manhattan 6.29 (slowest). Manhattan is the only borough faster in 2024 than in 2015 (+3%); Staten Island slowed most (-8%). The M42 crosstown is the single slowest route citywide at 5.27 mph (2025), and eight of the city's ten slowest routes are inside the congestion relief zone. Buses also fail to reach stops on schedule 30% of the time (37% for express buses).
subIndicators.source: NYC Comptroller, Bureau of Policy and Research, "Behind Schedule: How New York City's Bus System Slow Rolls Riders", April 2025 (Table 3 and Table 8), drawing on MTA bus speed data
subIndicators.reviewNote: All borough and citywide speeds confirmed digit-for-digit against Table 3 of the primary PDF. M42 corrected from 5.25 to 5.27 mph. The claim that NYC buses are 'the slowest of any major US city' was REMOVED: it appears nowhere in the cited report and could not be sourced to a primary comparative dataset.

subIndicators.name: Vision Zero traffic fatalities
subIndicators.value: 205 traffic deaths in 2025 -- the fewest ever recorded, dating back to when NYC record-keeping began in 1910, and one fewer than the previous record year (206 in 2018). Down 19% from 253 in 2024 and down 31% since Vision Zero launched in 2014. Pedestrian deaths 111 in 2025 vs. 122 in 2024 (-9%); child fatalities 6 vs. 16 (-63%); total injuries down 7.7% (47,557 vs 51,540) and serious injuries down 2.8% (2,947 vs 3,031). The improvement has continued: 42 deaths in the first three months of 2026, down 7% year-on-year and the third-fewest recorded at that point in the year since 1910 (only 2015 and 2018 were lower).
subIndicators.source: NYC DOT press releases, "Traffic Deaths Reach All-time Low" (January 2026) and "Traffic Deaths Are Near Lowest Levels in Recorded History After First Three Months of 2026"
subIndicators.reviewNote: MATERIAL CORRECTION FROM REVIEW. An earlier framing described recent years as 'among the deadliest of the Vision Zero era' and the dimension's level rationale treated traffic fatalities as a factor pushing severity upward. Primary NYC DOT sources refute that framing for the current period: 2025 is the safest year in recorded NYC history and Q1 2026 is the third-safest on record. Traffic safety is a verified STRENGTH of this dimension, not a shortfall, and is scored as such.

subIndicators.name: Fair Fares NYC enrollment vs. eligibility
subIndicators.value: About 385,000 of the 938,834 (~940,000) income-eligible New Yorkers are enrolled in the half-price transit fare program -- 41% of eligible, leaving 59% of eligible New Yorkers unenrolled. Eligibility is currently 150% of the Federal Poverty Level ($23,940 for a single adult, $49,500 for a household of four) for residents aged 18-64; adults 65+ and many disabled New Yorkers are excluded because they qualify for the MTA's separate Reduced-Fare program, and the Fair Fares discount does not apply to express buses. The threshold has risen from below 100% FPL at 2019 launch to 120% (2023) to 145% (2025) to 150%; in June 2026 the City Council and Mayor agreed to raise it to 200% FPL effective fall 2026, adding an estimated 342,604 newly eligible New Yorkers (total eligible rising to ~1.28 million). Earlier figure for trend: ~360,000 enrolled at end-2024 = 38% of eligible.
subIndicators.source: NYC Independent Budget Office, "Expanding Fair Fares: Many Options, A Range of Costs" (June 2026), based on IBO analysis of HRA enrollment data and ACS 2024 1-Year estimates; NYC Comptroller "Behind Schedule" (April 2025) for the end-2024 figure; NY1 (30 June 2026) for the 200% FPL agreement
subIndicators.reviewNote: CORRECTED IN REVIEW. The previous value ('~37% of the ~1.4 million income-eligible') was wrong on both numbers and internally impossible -- it implied ~518,000 enrollees, which no primary source supports. The 1.4 million figure is the eligible pool AFTER the future 200% FPL expansion, not the current one. The previous policy status ('145% FPL, with a further increase to 150% underway') was also stale: 150% is already in effect and 200% was agreed in June 2026. The under-enrollment shortfall is real but milder than previously stated and is closing.

subIndicators.name: NYC Streets Plan (LL195) mileage shortfall
subIndicators.value: DOT built 18.2 lane-miles of protected bike lanes in 2025 (36% of the 50-mile/year statutory minimum) and 13.5 lane-miles of protected bus lanes in 2024 (45% of the 30-mile/year minimum). 2024's ~29 bike-lane miles was reportedly the third-highest annual total in city history, yet still fell short of the legal mandate in every year checked.
subIndicators.source: City & State New York, "NYC DOT falls far short of '24 targets for bike and bus lanes" (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary DOT compliance filing in this review)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Not re-fetched in this review pass; confidence set to medium pending confirmation against NYC DOT's own Local Law 195 annual compliance reporting.

subIndicators.name: Congestion pricing (Central Business District Tolling Program / Congestion Relief Zone)
subIndicators.value: Launched 5 January 2025 at 12:00 AM. Current toll for Class 1 passenger vehicles with E-ZPass: $9.00 peak (5am-9pm weekdays, 9am-9pm weekends) and $2.25 overnight, per the TBTA tariff, which sets Phase 1 at 2025-2027 ($9.00/$2.25), Phase 2 at 2028-2030 ($12.00/$3.00) and Phase 3 from 2031 ($15.00/$3.75). A registered Low-Income Discount Plan halves the peak toll from the 11th trip in a calendar month. First-year measured effects (through ~November 2025): ~27 million fewer vehicle entries into the zone (11% average daily decline, ~73,000 fewer vehicles/day); vehicle miles travelled down 7.1%; morning-rush travel-time gains at major crossings (Holland Tunnel 51% faster, Queensboro Bridge 29.3%, Lincoln Tunnel 24.7%, Brooklyn Bridge 15%, Manhattan Bridge 6.7%); in-zone weekday vehicle speeds up 4%, weekend 6.2%, bus speeds 2.3%, truck speeds 5.6%; subway trips into the zone up 9%, express bus up 7.8%, local bus up 8.4%; $518M net toll revenue through November 2025 against a $500M/yr target, projected to exceed $550M. LITIGATION RESOLVED IN THE CITY'S FAVOUR: in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy (S.D.N.Y., filed 19 February 2025), Judge Lewis Liman granted the MTA a preliminary injunction in May 2025 and then, on 3 March 2026, issued a final 149-page decision holding that the federal administration lacked authority to terminate the program and that its attempted revocation of approval was arbitrary and capricious. Four other federal challenges (Chan, Mulgrew, New Yorkers Against Congestion Pricing Tax, Trucking Association) were closed on summary judgment for defendants on 17 April 2025. No court has ordered the program to halt, and it is operating.
subIndicators.source: MTA/TBTA CBD toll tariff (primary, for toll amounts and phase years); Governor Hochul first-anniversary release and MTA press releases (for measured first-year outcomes); Regional Plan Association congestion pricing litigation tracker and reporting on the 3 March 2026 ruling (for litigation status)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Toll amounts and phase years verified against the MTA primary tariff document. Litigation status updated in review: the previous entry stopped at the May 2025 preliminary injunction and missed the 3 March 2026 final ruling, which is the materially more significant outcome. A secondary claim circulating that congestion pricing is 'suspended by executive action' in 2026 was checked and is false.
subIndicators.geographicScaleNote: city (Manhattan CBD zone, with regional spillover effects)

subIndicators.name: Interborough Express (IBX)
subIndicators.value: Proposed 14-mile light-rail line connecting Brooklyn and Queens along an existing freight right-of-way, bypassing Manhattan; projected 160,000+ daily riders. As of 2026 the project is in design/environmental review; MTA estimates it would eliminate 21.8 million vehicle-miles of car trips annually once built. No construction start date confirmed.
subIndicators.source: MTA press release, Earth Day 2026 IBX vehicle-miles announcement; MTA project page (not independently re-verified in this review pass)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Not re-fetched in this review pass; confidence set to medium.

subIndicators.name: Sammy's Law / 20 mph speed limits
subIndicators.value: State legislation (Sammy's Law, 2024) authorized NYC for the first time to lower default speed limits without separate state approval. NYC DOT began lowering limits from 25 to 20 mph in 2024 and reported completing rollout across 250 designated zones/areas by the end of 2025.
subIndicators.source: News aggregation of NYC DOT rollout reporting (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary NYC DOT or NY State source in this review pass)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Confidence lowered to low: the only cited source is a news aggregator. A primary NYC DOT or NY State legislative citation is needed.

global.levelRationale: Scored null per ruling R2. The only quantified material available for this lens is a comparative construction-cost benchmark, which R2 explicitly rules out as a headline global indicator: 'NYC's subway construction costs are the highest in the world' is a governance and cost-efficiency fact about NYC, not a claim about NYC's effect on anyone beyond its boundary. That figure is retained below as a subIndicator. The genuinely global-facing threads -- NYC's transferability as the one large US city whose mode share is compatible with a 1.5C-aligned per-capita transport budget, the supply chains embodied in its rolling stock and electric bus fleet, and the aviation emissions of JFK/LaGuardia/Newark that sit outside the city's GPC inventory boundary -- are all real but none is quantified for NYC in this research pass. Per R2, an honest qualitative framing with a null level and named parties who could quantify it is the correct output; attaching a precise-looking score (the previous entry carried level 30 on no underlying quantity) would be a finding, not a result.
global.indicator: NYC's external mobility footprint and its transferability as a low-car megacity model -- qualitative pending quantification of (a) rolling-stock and electric-bus supply-chain sourcing, (b) aviation emissions excluded from the city inventory boundary, and (c) the transport-mode-share transferability argument
global.value: NOT QUANTIFIED. Three transmission channels are identified but none has a defensible NYC-specific number in this pass. (1) TRANSFERABILITY: NYC is the one large US city where a large majority of workers do not use a car to get to work (25.1% used a car, truck or van at all; 48.7% used public transit; 9.6% walked), which is the empirical basis on which dense transit-oriented development is argued globally to be compatible with a 1.5C per-capita transport budget. Quantifying NYC's per-capita transport emissions against a downscaled global transport budget would turn this into a real global indicator; that calculation has not been done here. (2) SUPPLY CHAIN: the embodied emissions and labour conditions in MTA rolling-stock procurement and electric-bus/battery sourcing are a genuine external footprint, but no NYC-specific quantification was located and this channel was not researched in this pass. (3) AVIATION: JFK, LaGuardia and Newark aviation emissions are widely reported to fall outside NYC's official GPC-protocol greenhouse-gas inventory boundary, which would make a substantial share of the mobility emissions NYC induces invisible in its own accounting. The primary source for this (Citizens Budget Commission) returned HTTP 403 on two separate fetch attempts, including during adversarial review, and the claim is therefore NOT asserted -- it remains a dataGap for MOCEJ and the Port Authority of NY & NJ to resolve. GLOBAL-EQUITY COUNTERPOINT (context, not an NYC-attributable metric): roughly 900 million to 1 billion rural people worldwide lack access to an all-season road (World Bank Rural Access Index / SDG indicator 9.1.1), a stark contrast with NYC's 24/7 rail system, but not something NYC policy moves.
global.target: No quantified target can be scored against until one of the three channels above is quantified. If NYC's per-capita transport emissions were computed, the appropriate benchmark would be a downscaled 1.5C-aligned per-capita transport budget applied identically across all portraits in the repo, consistent with rulings R8 and R12.
global.context: NYC's below-25%-car mode share is precisely the outcome climate and transit advocates worldwide point to as proof that dense transit-oriented cities work, and the city exports that model through comparative research and city networks (Transit Costs Project, ITDP, C40). The cost subIndicator below is the cautionary half of that story -- at $4B+ per mile NYC cannot build enough subway to close its own accessibility gaps -- but per R2 it describes NYC's governance, not NYC's effect on others, and so cannot carry this lens. The honest position is that mobility's global lens is currently unquantified, and that the fastest route to quantifying it is either the aviation-boundary question (MOCEJ / Port Authority) or a rolling-stock procurement footprint (MTA Construction & Development).
global.source: See subIndicators and dataGaps; no single source carries this lens.
global.productionVsConsumptionNote: not applicable as structured; the aviation-emissions boundary question is inherently a production-based-inventory-scope issue and could not be verified this pass

policyAnchors.name: Central Business District Tolling Program / Congestion Relief Zone (congestion pricing)
policyAnchors.relevance: Primary near-term lever changing NYC's mobility mode share and traffic volumes; direct funding source for the MTA capital accessibility program.
policyAnchors.status: Live and operating since 5 January 2025. Current Class 1 E-ZPass toll $9.00 peak / $2.25 overnight (tariff Phase 1, 2025-2027; $12.00 in Phase 2, 2028-2030; $15.00 from 2031). The federal attempt to terminate the program has FAILED on the merits: Judge Lewis Liman, S.D.N.Y., granted the MTA a preliminary injunction in May 2025 and issued a final 149-page ruling on 3 March 2026 in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy holding that the administration lacked authority to terminate and that the revocation was arbitrary and capricious. First-year outcomes (traffic down ~11%, VMT down 7.1%, faster crossings, $518M net revenue through November 2025) published by MTA and the Governor's office.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Streets Plan (Local Law 195 of 2019)
policyAnchors.relevance: Statutory minimum annual mileage for protected bus lanes (30 mi/yr) and protected bike lanes (50 mi/yr); the core accountability mechanism for street redesign.
policyAnchors.status: In effect but DOT has missed the mandate every recent year measured (2025: 18.2 mi bike lanes = 36% of mandate; 2024: 13.5 mi bus lanes = 45% of mandate). City Council was considering added tracking and oversight legislation as of April 2025. These figures rest on secondary reporting and should be confirmed against DOT's own LL195 compliance filings.

policyAnchors.name: MTA subway accessibility class-action settlement
policyAnchors.relevance: Binding, court-approved commitment on the pace of subway ADA accessibility upgrades -- the lever on the local-social lens's largest documented failure.
policyAnchors.status: Settlement in Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York v. MTA (NY State, 153765/2017) and De La Rosa v. MTA (S.D.N.Y., 19-cv-04406); fairness hearings April 2023. Commits the MTA to stair-free access at 95% of the 364 stations inaccessible at settlement by 2055, with interim milestones of +85 by 2035, +90 by 2045 and +90 by 2055 on top of 81 already contracted. 160 of 472 stations (33.9%) accessible as of July 2026, up from 108 at settlement and 154 at end-2025. The 2025-2029 Capital Program dedicates $7.1B to accessibility, targeting 60+ newly accessible stations this cycle.

policyAnchors.name: Sammy's Law (NY State, 2024)
policyAnchors.relevance: State authorization enabling NYC to set 20 mph default speed limits without prior state sign-off; directly supports Vision Zero.
policyAnchors.status: Reported as implemented, with DOT completing rollout of 20 mph limits across 250 designated zones by end of 2025. Sourced only to news aggregation in this pass -- needs a primary NYC DOT or NY State citation.

policyAnchors.name: Vision Zero (2014)
policyAnchors.relevance: The city's overarching traffic-safety policy framework; sets the baseline against which the record-low fatality counts are measured.
policyAnchors.status: Active and delivering. 2025 was the safest year in recorded NYC history (205 deaths, the fewest since record-keeping began in 1910, down 31% since the 2014 launch and one below the prior record of 206 in 2018). The first quarter of 2026 was the third-safest on record (42 deaths, down 7% year-on-year). This corrects an earlier characterization of recent years as among the era's deadliest.

policyAnchors.name: Fair Fares NYC
policyAnchors.relevance: City's primary transit-affordability program for low-income residents; the enrollment gap is a direct equity lever within the mobility dimension.
policyAnchors.status: Eligibility currently 150% FPL for residents aged 18-64; ~385,000 of ~940,000 eligible enrolled (41%). In June 2026 the City Council and Mayor agreed to raise the threshold to 200% FPL effective fall 2026, adding ~343,000 newly eligible (total eligible ~1.28M). The discount still does not apply to express buses, and adults 65+ and many disabled New Yorkers remain excluded because they qualify for the MTA's separate Reduced-Fare program.

social.comparisonNote: Petaluma's 72.6% drive-alone commute share (a small Mediterranean-climate city built almost entirely around cars) sits at nearly the opposite end of the spectrum from NYC's published 20.6% citywide figure -- and even NYC's most car-dependent borough, Staten Island, at 50.8%, is still well below Petaluma's rate. Both figures are ACS drive-alone shares of all workers 16+, including those who work from home, so they are directly comparable (R4). But the comparison cuts both ways: Petaluma has no subway to fail at accessibility, no multi-billion-dollar-per-mile construction-cost problem, and no decade-long traffic-safety programme comparable to Vision Zero. NYC's real failures here -- two-thirds of subway stations without stair-free access on a 2055 timetable, buses averaging 8.17 mph with no improvement in ten years, and 40.6-minute average commutes -- are failures of scale and complexity that a 60,000-person city never has to confront. Equally, NYC's traffic-safety record (fewest deaths since 1910) and its working congestion charge are achievements for which Petaluma has no equivalent lever.

NYC DOT's own Local Law 195 compliance filings, to replace the secondary reporting currently carrying the Streets Plan mileage-shortfall figures.

ecological.name: climate change
ecological.levelRationale: Scored under ruling R12 against the DEAL 1.5C-aligned per-capita benchmark (1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person), NOT against NYC's own 40x30 statutory target. NYC's production-based emissions are ~5.7 tCO2e/person (2024, DERIVED: 47,944,551 tCO2e / ~8,478,000 residents; the last officially published per-capita figure is 6.2 t for 2023) — roughly 3x the benchmark, so clearly overshooting the ceiling. Moderated from Petaluma's 100 (7.25 t) because NYC's per-capita is 15-20% lower and the trend is genuinely downward: -25.2% against the 2005 baseline, with CY2024 the largest single-year cut in the 20-year series. The adversarial reviewer recommended 40 by scoring against the 40x30 target; the orchestrator overrode that under R12 because the Doughnut's outer ring measures planetary boundaries, not statutory compliance, and a 40 here would have shown NYC almost inside the doughnut beside Petaluma at 100 for near-identical per-capita emissions.
ecological.indicator: NYC Citywide Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory (production-based, Citywide-GPC/BASIC methodology, 100-yr GWP, per Local Law 22 of 2008)
ecological.value: 47.94 MtCO2e citywide in 2024 (exact: 47,944,551 tCO2e) — down 25.2% from the 2005 baseline of 64.14 MtCO2e (64,139,721 tCO2e) and down 4.9% from 2023's 50.43 MtCO2e (50,433,720 tCO2e), the largest single-year reduction in the 20-year series. Per capita: MOCEJ's most recently published figure is 6.2 tCO2e/person (2023), which MOCEJ notes is 'over 50% lower than the 2020 U.S. average of 13 tCO2e per capita'; a CY2024 per-capita figure has not yet been published, and 47.94 Mt over the Census Bureau's Vintage-2024 July-2024 city population of 8,478,000 implies roughly 5.7 tCO2e/person (DERIVED here, not an official MOCEJ figure). Exact CY2024 sector shares: Stationary Energy (buildings) 69.5%, Transportation 26.3%, Waste 4.2%. (CY2023 for comparison: 71.2% / 24.9% / 3.9%; MOCEJ's own rounded slide labels for 2023 were 72%/25%/4%, which sum to 101%.)
ecological.target: Local Law 22 of 2008 mandates the Citywide-GPC inventory that tracks Local Law 97/PlaNYC goals: 40% reduction below 2005 levels by 2030 (MOCEJ slide: 'Carbon Reduction Targets: Citywide: 40% by 2030'), and carbon neutrality by 2050. NY State's CLCPA sets a parallel but distinct target (40% below 1990 by 2030, 85% by 2050, 70% renewable electricity by 2030), tracked via a separate 'Citywide-CLCPA' inventory that additionally counts fugitive energy-related emissions and uses a 20-yr GWP to highlight methane's near-term warming — carried as a subIndicator below, not averaged into the headline.
ecological.context:
⚠ Citywide figure shown — not specific to Manhattan. Not published; see Bronx note. Consumption-based CBEI proxy (different basis): Manhattan = 13 tCO2e/person (2019).

At 47.9 MtCO2e total, NYC's absolute footprint is roughly 110x Petaluma's (~0.435 MtCO2e) on about 141x the population, and its production-based per-capita figure of 6.2 tCO2e (2023, MOCEJ-published) is genuinely LOWER than Petaluma's 7.25 tCO2e/person (2024) — a real, counter-intuitive result driven by density, transit ridership, and small, efficient housing units. The policy lever is different in kind from a small city's: Local Law 97 imposes binding, penalty-backed emissions caps on nearly 50,000 covered properties, holding about 60% of the city's building floor area and about 50% of building-sector emissions (roughly 35% of citywide emissions), enforced property-by-property rather than through a single utility or fleet decision. The major recent complication is the April 2021 closure of the Indian Point nuclear plant, which MOCEJ's own analysis shows increased in-city fossil generation and grid carbon intensity (289.6 to 369.9 kg CO2/MWh, 2019-2023; renewables share of NYC's grid 36% to 14%; share of grid served by in-city plants 47% to 59%) and concentrated the resulting pollution increase in disadvantaged waterfront neighborhoods. MOCEJ also reports NYC as the second-largest total emitter among C40 cities, with its production-based per-capita emissions ranking 'just above average' among C40 members.

actions: If you sit on a co-op/condo board or manage a building over 25,000 sq ft, check your property's Local Law 97 filing status on NYC DOB's public compliance data and start a decarbonization plan now — Urban Green Council estimates 57% of covered properties already exceed the 2030 cap, and the penalty is $268 per metric ton over the limit.

Use NYC Accelerator (accelerator.nyc), the city's free technical-assistance program, to plan HVAC electrification retrofits, and look at the J51 tax abatement, which MOCEJ specifically flags as important for electrification projects to 'leapfrog' LL97 buildings off natural gas ahead of the 2030 caps.

Cut personal air travel and red-meat/dining-out consumption: per NYC's own Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory, air travel is 1.4 tCO2e per household — 34% of the average household's transportation footprint — and eating out plus animal products are nearly half of food emissions, which are themselves the single largest consumption category at 25% of the household total.

Push City Council and the Mamdani administration (in office since January 1, 2026) to fund LL97 enforcement and audits, protect the 2030 caps from weakening amendments, and advance large-scale renewable transmission (Champlain Hudson Power Express, offshore wind) — MOCEJ attributes 35% of the city's projected 2030 emissions progress to large-scale renewables, and project cancellations are the largest single risk to the target.

Support the Zero Waste Act's curbside organics program and use it consistently — MOCEJ lists landfilled waste as remaining constant even as wastewater-treatment efficiency has improved, and waste is 4.2% of citywide emissions.

If you live in a high-footprint tract — the CBEI's highest-emitting census tract is at 58 tCO2e/household against a citywide average of 29 and a lowest-tract figure of 18, a roughly 3-fold spread — prioritize reducing car ownership/VMT and air travel first. These are the categories where NYC households diverge most from a 1.5C-aligned per-capita budget, and the CBEI model identifies vehicle ownership and home size, not income alone, as the dominant drivers.

global.levelRationale: NYC's own Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory puts residents' household consumption emissions at 11 tCO2e/person (2019) — roughly 5.5x to 6.9x the ~1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person range DEAL cites as 1.5C-aligned, which is the benchmark this portrait scores the global lens against. That 11 t is a FLOOR, not a full account: the CBEI's own Appendix 4 states that government and institutional consumption, if allocated to households, would add 5.5 tCO2e per household (17.66 MtCO2e citywide, about +2.2 t/person, taking the figure to roughly 13 t); the inventory also excludes business and tourism consumption entirely and predates the post-Indian-Point grid deterioration. The trend is close to flat — down only 7.7% across 2007-2019 — against C40's finding that high-income cities must cut consumption emissions by two-thirds within a decade. Scored above 100 for cross-portrait consistency: the Petaluma portrait scores 100 at an overshoot of 3.6-4.5x the same benchmark, and NYC's consumption overshoot is roughly 1.5x larger, so an identical 100 would flatten a real difference. Held below 150 ('severe/emergency') because 11 tCO2e/person is about two-thirds of the US household average of 17 and is falling, if far too slowly, so the top of the scale stays reserved for footprints that are worst-in-class or rising.
global.indicator: NYC Household Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory (CBEI) — lifecycle/scope-3 emissions from NYC residents' household consumption of food, goods, housing, services and private transport, wherever in the world those emissions physically occur
global.value: 92 million MTCO2e for NYC household consumption in 2019 across 3,211,033 households — about 29 MTCO2e per household, or about 11 MTCO2e per person. SCOPE: household consumption by NYC residents only; the CBEI excludes business and tourism consumption, non-residential building energy, and government/institutional consumption. Category breakdown per household: Food 7.5 t (25% of the total; eating out 1.7 t and animal products 1.8 t, each about 23% of food emissions), Housing 7.0 t (natural gas 3.7 t, about 53% and the largest single component), Services 5.9 t (healthcare 3.4 t, 57%), Goods 4.2 t (furnishings and appliances 1.6 t, 38%), Private transportation 4.1 t (air travel alone 1.4 t, 34% of the transport share). Personal air travel citywide therefore totals roughly 4.5 million MTCO2e/year (DERIVED: 1.4 t/household x 3.21 million households) — and this captures only NYC residents' personal flights, not the far larger throughput of non-resident passengers transiting JFK/LaGuardia/Newark, which is not attributable to the city under this method. Emissions vary roughly 3-fold between census tracts: 58 tCO2e/household in the highest-emitting tract against 18 in the lowest, with the citywide average at 29.
global.target: DEAL's 1.5C-aligned per-capita consumption benchmark of roughly 1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person — the portrait's standing benchmark, used so severity is comparable across dimensions and across the Petaluma and NYC portraits. CONTEXT ONLY, NOT AN NYC TARGET: C40's 'The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5C World' (2019) Table 1 gives per-capita consumption trajectory figures for the 'North America, Oceania & High Income Asia' typology of 15.6 tCO2e/capita in 2017, 5.9 by 2030 and 0.7 by 2050. That is a REGIONAL-TYPOLOGY AVERAGE across the 21 cities C40 grouped into NYC's typology (Austin, Auckland, Boston, Chicago, Hong Kong, Houston, Los Angeles, Melbourne, Montreal, New Orleans, New York, Philadelphia, Portland, San Francisco, Seattle, Seoul, Sydney, Tokyo, Toronto, Vancouver, Washington), not a New York City commitment, and must never be presented as one. C40's qualitative requirement for this group is that 'high-income cities must decrease by two thirds within the next decade.'
global.context: This is the single most important entry in NYC's ecological portrait: it is the number that shows the small-city framing fails for a global megacity. THE FINDING, stated so it does not depend on a ratio: NYC residents' household consumption alone drives 92 MtCO2e/yr — 11 tCO2e per person — and the great majority of those emissions occur outside the five boroughs, entirely invisible to the territorial inventory that Local Law 97 and the 40x30 target are tracked against. MOCEJ puts it plainly: 'the vast majority of goods and services consumed in New York City are produced elsewhere. This means that most emissions in the CBEI are scope 3.' C40 quantifies the same channel network-wide: 85% of the emissions associated with goods and services consumed in C40 cities are generated outside the city — 60% elsewhere in the same country and 25% abroad. THE 67% COMPARISON, WITH ITS CAVEAT: the CBEI's own conclusion is that 92 MtCO2e is 'about 67% more than in the territorial inventory' (which it states as 55 MtCO2e for 2019), and that 'a CBEI that is much larger than a territorial inventory indicates that New York City is a net exporter of emissions.' Quote that as the source's own framing, with three qualifications. First, the two accountings are not a partition of the same universe: the CBEI counts only resident household consumption while the territorial inventory counts all in-boundary activity including commercial, industrial and freight, so the comparison is directional evidence rather than an arithmetic difference. Second, MOCEJ's own integration paper is explicit that the two inventories 'are developed using very different methods that are not directly compatible', and combining them into an Integrated Inventory required an estimated overlap correction — roughly 17 million MTCO2e of residential energy use is common to both. They must not be summed or subtracted. Third, the 55 MtCO2e territorial figure is a superseded vintage: the current NYC Open Data series puts CY2019 Citywide-GPC at 52.69 MtCO2e, against which 92 Mt is 75% larger. The cleanest single sentence for citation: NYC residents' household consumption footprint of 11 tCO2e/person is roughly 1.8x the entire city's territorial footprint per resident (about 6.3 tCO2e/person in 2019), even though the household figure counts only households. TRANSMISSION MECHANISMS: trade (food, goods, construction materials), personal aviation, institutional procurement, and finance — NYC-headquartered banks underwriting fossil-fuel projects worldwide, a separate channel the consumption inventory does not cover and which remains unquantified here. POLICY LEVER: categorically different from Local Law 97 — consumer behaviour, supply-chain standards such as the Good Food Purchasing Program, and national/global production decarbonisation NYC cannot mandate. C40's modelling credits city governments and urban stakeholders with delivering 35% of the necessary reductions on their own, and finds that meeting Deadline 2020 production-based commitments alone addresses the ~25% of consumption emissions that overlaps the territorial inventory and closes 80% of the consumption gap; the remainder depends on the carbon intensity of production worldwide.
global.source: NYC Household Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory (EcoDataLab with C40 Cities and MOCEJ, funded by American Express), 2019 base year, published February 2023; methodological relationship to the territorial inventory from MOCEJ, 'Integrating New York City's 2019 Citywide and Consumption Based Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventories'; global transmission figures from C40, 'The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5C World' (2019)

global.boroughsNote: The borough ranking is NOT a simple affluence gradient and should not be described as one: Staten Island is highest and the Bronx lowest, while Manhattan — the highest-income borough — sits mid-table on a per-household basis. This is real, not an artefact. The CBEI model scales national expenditure data on six household characteristics — household size, income, VEHICLE OWNERSHIP, HOME SIZE, educational attainment and home ownership — so car ownership and detached-housing floor area pull as hard as income. That is why the car-dependent, single-family outer borough tops the table and the transit-dependent, small-apartment inner borough sits at the bottom. Note also that per-capita and per-household rankings differ because household size varies: Manhattan ranks 4th of 5 per household but 2nd per capita.

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 97 of 2019
policyAnchors.relevance: Binding, penalty-backed building emissions caps on nearly 50,000 covered properties (buildings over 25,000 gross sq ft, plus multi-building tax lots and condo boards over 50,000 sq ft), holding about 60% of NYC's building floor area and about 50% of building-sector emissions — roughly 35% of citywide emissions. A 2024-2029 compliance period is followed by a much tighter 2030-2034 cap; penalty is $268 per metric ton over the limit.
policyAnchors.status: First compliance-period reports (calendar year 2024) were due Dec 31, 2025. Per DOB's April 22, 2026 release, approximately 93% of covered privately owned properties, representing 91% of covered buildings, filed; roughly 1,400 properties failed to file and received Notices of Deficiency. DOB is still auditing the filings and has NOT yet published cap-compliance rates — it says it will do so later in 2026. Urban Green Council's independent modelling from CY2024 benchmarking data estimates about 9% of properties exceed their 2024-2029 cap but about 57% already exceed the 2030 cap. CY2025 reports are due May 1, 2026 and annually thereafter, with a grace period through June 30.

ecological.comparisonNote: Counter-intuitively, NYC's production-based per-capita footprint (6.2 tCO2e/person, 2023, MOCEJ-published; roughly 5.7 derived for 2024) is LOWER than Petaluma's 7.25 tCO2e/person (2024), driven by density, transit ridership and small, efficient housing — even though NYC's absolute emissions of 47.9 MtCO2e (2024) are roughly 110x Petaluma's ~0.435 MtCO2e on about 141x the population. Note that the two portraits score this dimension against different targets: Petaluma's local level is set against the DEAL 1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person benchmark, whereas NYC's local level is set against NYC's own statutory 40%-below-2005-by-2030 target, which is why the wedges differ more than the underlying per-capita figures do. NYC's consumption-based footprint (11 tCO2e/person, 2019) is where the comparison genuinely flips: it captures the embodied carbon in everything the city imports and consumes, which a small-city inventory like Petaluma's does not attempt to measure at all. It is this global/consumption lens — not the production lens — where NYC's status as a global financial and consumption centre actually shows up.

ecological.name: nitrogen & phosphorus loading
ecological.levelRationale: NYC still discharges ~18 billion gallons/year of untreated combined sewage through 398 outfalls (CSO), and the city has missed its first two green-infrastructure milestones (1.5% by 2015, 4% by 2020, against a 2030 goal), which argues for 'needs attention.' That is offset by genuinely large, verified nitrogen-specific point-source gains (>58% cut at the four East River WRRFs, ~50%+ cut into Jamaica Bay since 2010) and a harbor-wide dissolved-oxygen record that has been above the NYS 5.0 mg/L standard every summer since the 1990s — real, monitored improvement a small-city groundwater-nitrate problem like Petaluma's does not have an equivalent to.
ecological.indicator: Combined sewer overflow (CSO) annual discharge volume, paired with wastewater nitrogen loading to receiving waters
ecological.value: Wards Island WRRF (administratively Manhattan/Randall's Island, discharges to the Upper East River/Long Island Sound): nitrogen upgrade completed, cutting discharge from 33,000 lbs/day to 17,000 lbs/day (~48% reduction).
ecological.target: Reduce CSO volume by 1.67 billion gallons/year by 2040 and spend $3.5B on green infrastructure by 2045 (2023 CSO Consent Order Modification, DEC Case CO2-20110512-25 modifying CO2-20000107-8). Nitrogen: Long Island Sound TMDL (EPA-approved 2001) requires an aggregate 58.5% reduction in human-generated nitrogen vs. a 1990 baseline; the 2010 Jamaica Bay Nitrogen Consent Agreement targeted ~50% reduction in WRRF nitrogen loading to the bay.
ecological.context:
Manhattan: Wards Island WRRF (administratively Manhattan/Randall's Island, discharges to the Upper East River/Long Island Sound): nitrogen upgrade completed, cutting discharge from 33,000 lbs/day to 17,000 lbs/day (~48% reduction).

Citywide for comparison: ~18 billion gallons/year of combined sewage discharged citywide through 398 CSO outfalls (~60% of NYC is combined-sewered). Nitrogen: the four East River WRRFs (Wards Island, Hunts Point, Bowery Bay, Tallman Island) cut aggregate nitrogen discharge by >58% after a $1B+ upgrade program; the four Jamaica Bay WRRFs (Jamaica, 26th Ward, Coney Island, Rockaway) cut nitrogen loading to Jamaica Bay from a historic ~54,000 lbs/day to a currently reported ~18,000-20,000 lbs/day.

This is a wastewater-and-CSO story, not an agricultural-runoff story — the sharp structural contrast with Petaluma, where the same dimension is scored on groundwater nitrate near farms and septic systems. NYC's 14 WRRFs and 398 combined-sewer outfalls mean nitrogen and pathogen loading are concentrated at engineered point sources tied to rain events, not diffuse land-based leaching. The policy levers are capital-intensive: WRRF biological nutrient removal retrofits (East River, Jamaica Bay), CSO storage tunnels (Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay), and the green infrastructure program, which the city is currently behind schedule on. Caveat: the citywide 18 BGY figure and the 398-outfall count are the most current published DEP/DEC figures, but a single up-to-date, citywide nitrogen-loading total across all 14 WRRFs (as opposed to per-facility figures of varying vintage) was not found in this search.

global.levelRationale: No NYC-specific quantified nitrogen- or phosphorus-footprint study was located, so this level rests on a proxy: nitrogen is one of the planetary boundaries scientists (Steffen et al. 2015, Rockström et al.) consider already transgressed globally at a 'high risk' level via synthetic fertilizer use, and NYC's food supply is entirely import-dependent on that globally overshot system. That directional judgment supports a 'needs attention'-to-'critical' score, but the lack of a city-specific number keeps me from placing it higher with confidence.
global.indicator: NYC's embodied/consumption-based nitrogen footprint via its imported food supply (no verified city-specific study found; scaled from national per-capita averages as an order-of-magnitude proxy)
global.value: Not directly measured for NYC. The U.S. average per-capita nitrogen footprint is reported as roughly 30-41 kg N/person/year (dominated by food production), per the N-Print project (University of Virginia). Applying that national average to NYC's ~8.3M residents implies a rough order-of-magnitude footprint of roughly 250,000-340,000 metric tons N/year — this is an extrapolation from a national figure, not a measured NYC number, and should be treated as illustrative only.
global.target: No NYC-specific target exists. The relevant global anchor is the planetary nitrogen boundary itself: Steffen et al. (2015) put the safe boundary for anthropogenic nitrogen fixation at 62-82 Tg N/year, against actual global fixation estimated at roughly 150 Tg N/year (already substantially overshot).
global.context: NYC's nitrogen and phosphorus footprint is transmitted globally through its food system: importing produce, grain, meat, and dairy from farms that use synthetic fertilizer manufactured from mined phosphate rock (a finite resource concentrated in Morocco/Western Sahara) and fossil-fuel-derived nitrogen. A 2020 peer-reviewed 'community nitrogen footprint' methodology applied to Baltimore City (~19,000 metric tons N/year, ~30 kg N/capita/year, 73% from food production) is the closest published municipal-scale analog and shows this kind of analysis is feasible for a U.S. city; it has not, to my knowledge, been done for NYC. Separately, NYC exports its wastewater biosolids (roughly 500,000+ tons/year across all 14 WRRFs) largely to landfill and historically to out-of-state land application (Colorado, Florida, 1992-2010); each ton landfilled instead of land-applied represents phosphorus that is not being returned to agricultural soils, a lost-recovery issue tied to the finite global phosphate-rock reserve.

ecological.name: land conversion
ecological.levelRationale: 50 is defensible if and only if the dimension is scored purely as canopy-versus-goal, but it is too high once the target is stated accurately and the orchestrator's density ruling is applied. On the target: Local Law 148's 30% is statutory but carries NO deadline; 2040 is an administrative date chosen in April 2026 and 2035 was never in the law. So the sharpest negative available — 'the city has blown a legal deadline' — does not exist. What does exist: 23.4% is 78% of the way to the goal; canopy rose in all five boroughs 2017-2021 (+1.2 pts, ~+0.3 pts/yr); at that rate 30% arrives around 2043, and press analysis of the 2026 plan puts it at 2055 or later on current funding, with Comptroller Levine (April 2026) finding forested natural areas get ~0.7% of the Parks expense budget. Against that, on land conversion proper NYC is close to neutral-positive: the city is built out, its 2024 rezoning (City of Yes, 82,000 homes) adds capacity by infill rather than by extending the built footprint, per-capita land consumption is the lowest of major US cities (~459 m2/person), 14% of city land is NYC parkland, and the orchestrator has ruled the density is genuinely land-conserving at regional scale. The remaining genuine problems are a 7-point EJ canopy gap (19% vs 26%), net canopy loss on one- and two-family residential lots concentrated in southeastern Queens, and largely irreversible historic wetland loss (Jamaica Bay 2,350 acres of marsh islands in 1951 to ~800 today, only ~60 acres restored at Elders Point). That profile is worse than 'on track' (0) but well short of a full 'needs attention' (50): 25 is the honest placement. I flag for the orchestrator that this is a disagreement about indicator scope, not about any number — the canopy data and the borough data both survived verification intact.
ecological.indicator: Tree canopy cover % (citywide), with parkland %, impervious surface %, and wetland loss/restoration as supporting sub-indicators
ecological.target: Local Law 148 of 2023 (Admin. Code s 18-164) sets a statutory goal of equitably expanding tree canopy to 30% of city land area. NOTE: the statute sets NO deadline — the commonly cited 2040 date is an administrative target, not a legal one.
ecological.context:
Manhattan: 22.7% tree canopy (2021)

Citywide for comparison: 23.4% canopy citywide (45,247 acres) in 2021, up from 22.2% (2017) and 20.37% (2010); ~72% of the city's 305 sq mi land area is impervious surface (buildings, roads, sidewalks); NYC Parks manages >30,000 acres = 14% of city land as parkland, rising to ~19.5% (38,000–50,000 acres) if state/federal parkland within the five boroughs is included

Unlike Petaluma, where 'land conversion' means whether farmland/open space outside an urban growth boundary gets paved over, NYC is already ~72% impervious — the meaningful question is how much of the remaining pervious/natural fraction is protected, growing, or being lost, and whether the city's own growth model (infill density) is itself averting conversion elsewhere. Nearly 90% of 2017–2021 canopy growth came from existing trees expanding rather than new plantings, and the only net canopy LOSS citywide was on one- and two-family residential lots, concentrated in southeastern Queens — meaning small-lot residential development/hardscaping is the marginal driver of loss even in a built-out city. The policy lever is Local Law 148 implementation funding (flagged as under-resourced by the City Comptroller) plus zoning/permitting practices for residential lot coverage. Caveat: canopy %, parkland %, and impervious % measure related but distinct things and none alone is a perfect proxy; we present all three rather than picking one number to represent 'land conversion' for a megacity.

This footprint is transmitted through supply chains (imported beef, soy-fed livestock products, palm oil in packaged food, tropical hardwoods and paper), not through direct land conversion within the five boroughs. It is conceptually the land-use analog to the well-documented gap between NYC's production-based GHG inventory and its higher consumption-based footprint. No source was found that isolates NYC (or even the NY metro) from national U.S. per-capita averages, so any NYC-specific number here would be an estimate presented as fact — instead this is flagged as a research gap. NYC's ~200,000+ acres of protected upstate watershed land (Catskill/Delaware system) is the one large, well-quantified land-protection footprint NYC holds outside its own boundaries, but it protects drinking-water quality rather than offsetting consumption-driven deforestation, so it is reported here for completeness rather than folded into a global-footprint number.

ecological.name: air pollution
ecological.levelRationale: The headline alone supports something close to 25: DOHMH's published citywide annual mean of 6.26 µg/m³ (2024) is 25% above the WHO 2021 guideline of 5 µg/m³, no NYC county is designated nonattainment for PM2.5, monitor design values run 7.7-8.3 against a 9.0 NAAQS, and the trend is strongly favourable (PM2.5 −36%, NO2 −41%, black carbon −56%, SO2 −98% since 2009). Per R1 the level must then be adjusted for well-sourced shortfalls inside the same dimension, and there are four material ones. (1) Ozone: all five boroughs sit in 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment with an August 3, 2027 attainment deadline, and NYCCAS shows no downward ozone trend at all (24.3 ppb in 2009 to 32.3 ppb in 2024) with DOHMH expecting it to worsen with warming — a dimension cannot be 'mild' when the region formally fails a health standard and the failing pollutant is flat-to-rising. (2) Mortality and morbidity burden: DOHMH attributes ~2,000 excess deaths/yr (1 in 25 deaths citywide) to long-term PM2.5, with a modelled 1,798 deaths/yr age 30+ and 1,125 pediatric asthma ED visits/yr in the 2017-2019 vintage. (3) Distributional failure: child asthma ED visits range from 441.8 per 10,000 in Brownsville to 20.6 in Tottenville–Great Kills (2023), roughly 21x, and Manhattan's PM2.5 (7.71) is 30% above Queens's (5.95) with Midtown at 10.5 — the citywide mean conceals an exposure gradient the dimension exists to show. (4) Episodic overshoot: two severe wildfire-smoke events in three years (AQI 465 in June 2023, AQI 289 across five days in July 2026 alongside a heat emergency), and the 2023 citywide regulatory-monitor annual average of 10.8 µg/m³ exceeded the federal standard outright. On the other side, R5 forbids manufacturing a crisis: this is a city with a genuine multi-decade improvement record, the most granular urban monitoring network in the US, and a documented policy win in the residual-oil phase-out. 100 would be doom inflation and 25 launders the ozone failure and the mortality burden. 50 — 'needs attention' — is the honest reading. The global lens stays at 50: the outbound channels are now quantified (port share of county NOx up to 17.5%, the only tri-state monitor above the 9.0 NAAQS sitting inside the port complex at 9.4 µg/m³, and NY-source contributions above 14 ppb on Connecticut's worst ozone days), so R2's requirement for quantification is met and a score rather than null is justified.

global.levelRationale: NYC cannot unilaterally control two of the three largest pressures on its air-pollution ceiling: (1) upwind/interstate ozone-precursor transport, part of why the NY-NJ-CT region was reclassified from 'Moderate' to 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment in July 2024 despite the city's own local control measures, and (2) increasingly frequent transboundary Canadian wildfire smoke (2023, recurring 2024 and again mid-July 2026) that is itself a downstream effect of global climate change. Layered on top, the Port of NY/NJ — the busiest port on the US East Coast — services NYC-area (and much wider) consumption demand and its ocean-going vessels alone account for 53% of the port's NOx and 36% of its PM2.5 emissions, a footprint driven by global containerized trade rather than by New Yorkers' local combustion. 'Needs attention' reflects a real, evidenced overshoot with only partial local leverage, not an unquantified hand-wave.

global.context: NYC's air-pollution footprint is not a closed local system. Regionally, the metro area's persistent ozone problem is driven substantially by NOx and VOC transport from upwind states and the wider Ozone Transport Region, which is why New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut jointly petitioned for and received the 2024 'Serious' reclassification rather than fixing it through city-level action alone — this is the ozone-pollution analogue to a 'consumption-based' emissions argument in the climate dimension. Separately, the Port of NY/NJ exists to serve import/export demand — much of it NYC consumption — and its ocean-going vessels, drayage trucks, and cargo-handling equipment emit PM2.5 and NOx concentrated in South Bronx, Red Hook, and New Jersey waterfront communities that host the region's port and last-mile e-commerce warehouse infrastructure. And the escalating frequency of Canadian wildfire smoke intrusions (2023, 2024, and again mid-July 2026) means an increasing share of NYC's worst PM2.5 days now originates entirely outside city and even national jurisdiction, tied to boreal-forest climate change. Aviation (JFK, LaGuardia, Newark) is a further plausible contributor to both local NOx/PM near the airports and to NYC's share of global aviation emissions, but no single quantified 'NYC aviation air-pollution footprint' figure was located in this research pass.

ecological.name: heat & climate resilience
ecological.levelRationale: BENCHMARK NOTE (R12): this is one of the two locally-defined ecological dimensions (R6). There is no Raworth planetary boundary for urban heat mortality and no DEAL downscaled per-capita benchmark, so R12's instruction to score against the framework benchmark has no direct analogue. The benchmark scored against is stated explicitly: ZERO PREVENTABLE HEAT DEATHS. That is the defensible framework-equivalent because DOHMH itself frames these deaths as preventable and the dominant risk factor is a purchasable good — home AC and the ability to run it — rather than an irreducible meteorological hazard; and unlike a city statute it applies identically to any portrait, which is R12's actual purpose. ANCHOR: ~500 heat-related deaths/year, about 3% of all warm-season deaths, heat being NYC's deadliest weather hazard, against a benchmark of zero. PUSHED UP BY (R1): the direct heat-stress racial disparity has WIDENED rather than closed in the current vintage — Black New Yorkers at 3x the white age-adjusted rate (1.2 vs 0.4 per million, 2016-2025) against 2x in the previous vintage — nine years after Cool Neighborhoods NYC (2017) made closing it an explicit aim; 2025 produced 21 heat-stress deaths, the highest single-year tally in over a decade, 19 of them in one four-day June heat wave, and 18 of the 21 decedents were Black or Latino; ~493,000 rental households have AC they do not run because of utility cost, so ownership statistics overstate real protection; the most heat-vulnerable neighbourhood citywide by HVI, East Flatbush (85% Black), has 1.2 cooling centres per 100,000 residents against Manhattan's 7.1. PULLED DOWN BY, but insufficient to move the score: citywide AC penetration of ~90-91% is genuinely high and is reported as such per R5; Local Law 128 of 2025 now makes a 7-per-100,000 cooling-centre target statutory with a plan due 15 May 2026; Local Law 41 of 2021 requires resilient design across the ~$90B city capital portfolio from 2026; CoolRoofs has coated more than 10M sq ft since 2009. Those are inputs, not outcomes, and the outcome measure has not improved. Not raised to 150 (emergency) because programmes exist and are expanding and the toll is not accelerating on a like-for-like basis. Level 100 (Critical) retained.
ecological.indicator: Heat-related mortality (direct heat-stress deaths + modelled heat-exacerbated deaths)
ecological.value: ~500 heat-related deaths per year citywide, May-September — about 3% of all warm-season deaths (2026 New York City Heat-Related Mortality Report, DOHMH, released 15 June 2026). This is a MULTI-YEAR ANNUAL AVERAGE, not a single-year count: an average of 7 direct heat-stress deaths/year (pooled 2016-2025) plus an average of ~490 modelled heat-exacerbated deaths/year (pooled 2014-2023), where heat aggravates an existing condition. EQUITY — SCOPE STATED PRECISELY: DOHMH's race-disaggregated rates cover DIRECT HEAT-STRESS DEATHS ONLY. For 2016-2025 the age-adjusted heat-stress death rate was 1.2 per million for Black New Yorkers and 1.0 for Latino New Yorkers against 0.4 for white New Yorkers — 3x and 2x respectively, in DOHMH's own words 'Black New Yorkers had heat-stress death rates three times higher and Latino New Yorkers had death rates two times higher than white New Yorkers.' DOHMH publishes NO race-disaggregated rate for the ~490/year heat-exacerbated component that makes up ~98% of the headline; for that component its inequity finding is qualitative ('inequitably affects Black New Yorkers, reflecting the impacts of structural racism'). The ratio and the headline therefore describe different populations and must not be conflated. Corroborating single-year fact: in 2025, 21 New Yorkers died of heat stress — the highest tally in over a decade, 19 of them during one four-day June heat wave — and 18 of the 21 were Black or Latino.
ecological.target: No codified numeric mortality target exists, and no planetary boundary applies to this locally-defined dimension. The benchmark used for scoring is ZERO PREVENTABLE HEAT DEATHS plus elimination of the racial disparity in heat mortality — the aim DOHMH and Cool Neighborhoods NYC (2017) state in qualitative terms, pursued via AC access and affordability, cooling centres, tree canopy and cool roofs. Statutory commitments that exist (Local Law 41 of 2021 on resilient capital design; Local Law 128 of 2025's 7-cooling-centres-per-100,000 target) are progress measures reported in context and policyAnchors, never the scoring anchor.
ecological.context:
⚠ Citywide figure shown — not specific to Manhattan. PROXY ONLY — no borough-level heat-mortality rate is published, per R10. Closest proxies, each measuring something other than the headline: Central Harlem is Manhattan's HVI-5 neighbourhood in the Comptroller's list (a MODELLED VULNERABILITY COMPOSITE), in sharp intra-borough contrast with the low-HVI Upper East and Upper West Sides; Manhattan has the citywide-highest cooling-centre density at 7.1 per 100,000 (a FACILITY-SUPPLY measure), which masks that internal disparity. Note: East Harlem is often described as highly heat-vulnerable and received new cooling capacity under the 2026 report, but it does not appear in the Comptroller's HVI-5 list and no HVI-5 attribution for it was verified.

In an 8.3M-person city, heat kills more people annually than all other weather hazards combined, and the mechanism is overwhelmingly indoor and socioeconomic (un-air-conditioned homes, and AC that households cannot afford to run) rather than purely meteorological — sharply different from Petaluma's wildfire-smoke-centered climate-health narrative. VINTAGE LADDER (R11), all confirmed from primary sources: the 2022 report (released 16 June 2022) gave ~370 deaths/year with race rates for 2011-2020 (Black 2.2 vs white 0.9 per million, 2x); the 2025 report (released 30 June 2025) gave ~525/year pooled 2018-2022, of which ~5/year heat-stress and ~520/year heat-exacerbated, with race rates for 2014-2023 (Black 0.8 vs white 0.4, 2x); the 2026 report gives ~500/year with race rates for 2016-2025 (Black 1.2, Latino 1.0, white 0.4, i.e. 3x and 2x). The step from ~370 to ~500-525 is driven principally by a moved pooling window and by DOHMH's successive refinements to the heat-exacerbated excess-mortality model — it is a methodology and scope shift, NOT a measured trend, and the portrait must not read it as a rise; note the current ~500 is in fact BELOW the previous vintage's ~525. The widening of the Black:white direct heat-stress ratio from 2x to 3x reflects the June 2025 heat wave entering the pooling window. The policy lever is AC access and its affordability (utility cost, not just ownership), tree canopy in redlined/EJ neighborhoods, and building-level cooling requirements; Local Law 97's building-emissions caps and heat-pump retrofit push interact with this because electrified cooling raises electricity demand even as it cuts direct heat-stress risk.

actions: Apply early for the NY State HEAP Cooling Assistance Benefit via ACCESS NYC or OTDA each spring — funds are first-come-first-served and the 2026 benefit closed on 5 June, so late applicants are shut out for the whole summer. Note you are ineligible if your household received a HEAP-funded AC within the past five years.

During a heat emergency, use NYC Emergency Management's Cooling Center Finder or call 311 to locate the nearest cooling center (library, community or senior center, or NYCHA facility) under the Local Law 85/128 network.

If you live in a basement or cellar apartment, check eligibility for the city's basement and cellar legalization pilot (Local Law 126 of 2024) through DOB/HPD before the 20 April 2029 deadline — but note flood-prone properties are excluded from the programme, so know your flood-evacuation route regardless, given the Hurricane Ida basement-death pattern.
Support or join the NYC Environmental Justice Alliance's (NYC-EJA) Extreme Heat & Air Quality campaign, which pushes for equitable cooling-center density and canopy investment in HVI-5 neighborhoods.

In the South Bronx, connect with or volunteer for the Be A Buddy program (run by The Point CDC in Hunts Point) which does neighbor check-ins for isolated, heat-vulnerable residents during extreme-heat days.

Hold NYCEM to Local Law 128 of 2025: the comprehensive cooling and communication plan was due on or before 15 May 2026 and the law sets a target of no fewer than 7 cooling centers per 100,000 residents — compare that against your own neighborhood's actual count.

Track your community board's Cloudburst/Stormwater Resiliency Plan timeline and the NY-NJ Harbor & Tributaries Study public comment process (Army Corps/DEP), since both determine whether and when your neighborhood gets flood infrastructure.
